entries.title: 4-year-old in critical condition after being shot in the head
entries.summary: <p>A 4-year-old boy is in critical condition after he was shot in the head in South Deering Tuesday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Officers responded to a residence in the 2200 block of East 99th Street at 4:01 p.m. and found the boy, police said. He was taken to Comer Children’s Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>No one is in custody and an investigation is ongoing into the incident, police said. </p>

entries.title: White Sox anticipating raucous crowd, seek to clinch first postseason-series victory at home since 1906
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> played their last home game a week and a half ago.</p><p>They fended off the Rockies and were cheered for a successful regular season that resulted in their highest home attendance in four years (1.986 million). For a marquee MLB franchise, that figure might represent a crisis. But it was well above the threshold where the Sox felt supported.</p><p>‘‘The most simple way to put what is special about our club is the enthusiasm on the field,’’ manager Will Venable said. ‘‘When you’re a player and there’s no one in the stands, you kind of question who you are. When you’re on the field and there’s a bunch of people there, that gives you confidence that you’re a good club that people are paying good money to come see.’’</p><p>But as the sixth seed in the American League playoffs, the Sox left town last week not knowing whether they would play in Chicago again this year. It was an irksome notion.</p><p>‘‘Our fans, they deserve baseball in October,’’ All-Star third baseman Miguel Vargas said.</p><p>Vargas is one of the few players on hand who has observed the Sox’ progression from the losingest MLB team of all time in 2024 to a team a victory away from reaching the AL Championship Series next week. There has been enough turnover for this to feel like an entirely new project.</p><p>‘‘There is a big change in personnel; this is a very, very different team,’’ said right-hander Erick Fedde, who was also on the 2024 club. ‘‘A lot of new faces to create the success.’’</p><p>Surely, there has been a new crop of viewers drawn to a team that socked 211 home runs this season and produces at least one viral video clip per week. By and large, however, the Sox’ fan base simply has endured the wait for meaningful baseball.</p><p>For that reason, ensuring a home playoff game was a rallying cry for the Sox, something celebrated in the locker room in Houston after a sweep of the wild-card series.</p><p>‘‘We’re expecting the most rowdy crowd I’ve ever played before in my entire life,’’ said right-hander Sean Burke, who made his big-league debut in 2024.</p><p>With the Sox’ two victories in Cleveland, however, the scale of potential happenings this week at Rate Field has increased again.</p><p>The 2005 Sox clinched all three of their playoff-series victories, as well as their division title, on the road. When the 1959 Sox clinched the AL pennant, prompting Chicago Fire Commissioner Robert Quinn to turn on the air-raid sirens, the team was in Cleveland. That might explain why so many people were startled. No Sox team has locked down the final victory of a playoff series in front of its home fans since the club won the World Series in 1906.</p><p>‘‘One hundred twenty years?’’ surprised reliever Grant Taylor said. ‘‘Maybe we can do it this year.’’</p><p>Maybe a historic release of fan energy is the key ingredient. By the admission of the players and coaches, the Sox have been more comfortable as an underdog than as a front-runner. A slate of road playoff games as the lower seed found them back in a comfortable mindset. They could use an extra jolt.</p><p>‘‘That is definitely true that we have a lot of comfort in being the underdog; that is the story of this club,’’ Venable said. ‘‘I don’t think any of it matters. We get to play a playoff game at home, and that’s all these guys are really thinking about.’’</p><p>While the 20-somethings on the roster might be light on their franchise history, they know the environment that awaits them doesn’t come easily or often.</p><p>‘‘This could be a once-in-a-lifetime thing for us,’’ outfielder Tristan Peters said. ‘‘You’ve got to be excited.’’</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/06/chicago-white-sox-rivals-cleveland-guardians-will-venable-stephen-vogt-sam-antonacci-sean-newcomb-jordan-hicks-brewers-tigers-twins-bulls-cavaliers" >White Sox need a rival, and Guardians fit the bill — they just have to dislike each other</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/06/white-sox-have-leaned-into-their-strengths-will-heavy-bullpen-use-but-change-is-coming-will-venable-chris-getz-erick-fedde-sean-newcomb-sean-burke-munetaka-murakami" >White Sox have leaned into strengths with heavy bullpen use, but change is coming</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Man sentenced to 15 years for selling gun to undercover cop used in fatal shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man has been sentenced to 15 years in federal prison for selling an undercover Chicago police officer a gun he had used to fatally shoot a man in Greater Grand Crossing, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Illinois.</p><p>Levion Thomas was sentenced last Thursday by U.S. District Judge Thomas M. Durkin after pleading guilty to a federal illegal firearm possession charge in 2024, according to the federal office.</p><p>The gun Thomas possessed had been tied to the murder of Troy Pouncey, 31, who was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2023/3/5/23626332/man-shot-to-death-greater-grand-crossing" target="_blank" ><u>shot</u></a> in his face and body around 1:15 p.m. in the 7100 block of South Calumet Avenue March 5, 2023, according to Chicago police. He was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center where he later died.</p><p>The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, along with Chicago police, arranged for a purchase of the weapon by an undercover officer after finding Thomas had been looking to sell the weapon, prosecutors said in court documents.</p><p>Thomas sold the gun, which he used to kill Pouncey, to an undercover Chicago police officer in the front seat of a car in Burnham, Illinois, 15 days after the shooting.</p><p>Thomas initially got into the vehicle wearing a mask before removing it, which revealed his face to the cameras inside the car. He then took $500 in exchange for the handgun, per court documents. Thomas had previously pleaded guilty to a charge of aggravated unlawful use of a weapon in 2021, for which he was sentenced to a year in prison.</p><p>“Too many people in this city believe that they can unlawfully possess firearms with impunity,” Assistant U.S. Attorneys Julia Schwartz and Jessica Ecker wrote in court documents. “This needs to stop.”</p>

entries.title: Sales surge for businesses near Rate Field as White Sox gears up for Game 3
entries.summary: <p>A line of more than 20 customers stood outside of sports retail store Grandstand before it opened Tuesday at 10 a.m, but co-owners Josh and Stephanie Ganal weren't surprised. </p><p>The store at 600 W. 35th St., a few blocks from Rate Field, has been flooded with enthusiastic <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> fans for weeks. And business has ramped up even more ahead of Wednesday's Game 3 of the American League Division Series.</p><p>If the Sox win, it would be their first time in the American League Championship Series since 2005.</p><p>Businesses near Rate Field, like Grandstand, have seen record foot traffic and sales, along with a joyful mob of fans.</p><p>“It’s very similar [to 2005],” Josh Ganal said of the excitement. “I think the only difference is that time we were expected to be there. This time, it's exciting to be there.”</p><p>The last few seasons have been tough for the Sox, with three years of at least 100 losses, plus an MLB record of 121 losses in 2024.</p><p>“Nobody was really expecting this team to come out as good as they are,” Josh Ganal said. “It's a different team entirely. They’re fun to watch. You can't ever count them out, and it's good for the city. It rejuvenates a totally different era of fans.”</p><p>He said this year's team roster is full of personality and camaraderie.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Benet's Gene Heidkamp tops our list of high school basketball coaching awards
entries.summary: <p>With local high school boys basketball coaches a month away from welcoming their teams back into the gym to start practicing for the upcoming season, here’s a look at who could be considered the best among them in several categories:</p><h3><b>Best coach: Gene Heidkamp, Benet</b></h3><h3></h3><p>It’s hard to look at Heidkamp’s 18 years at Benet and argue for anyone else. Benet basketball has a profound identity, credited largely to a coach held in the highest respect by colleagues and counterparts.</p><p>There’s also the obvious: results.</p><p>Heidkamp has built arguably the best program in the state — a model of consistency with a winning percentage of 74% over nearly two decades. His Redwings brought home a state championship in March 2025 after runner-up finishes in 2014, 2016, 2023, and were runners-up again last season.</p><h3><b>Best coach without a state title: Mike Ellis, Evanston</b></h3><h3></h3><p>In 23 years, Ellis has accumulated more than 500 career victories while leading two powerhouses in Peoria Richwoods and Evanston. He has done everything but win a state title, although he has been close with five state tournament appearances, including runner-up finishes in 2006 and 2010 with Richwoods and 2019 with Evanston, as well as eight sectional championships.</p><p>His Wildkits have the potential to capture another trophy in Champaign in March, possibly taking Ellis off the list of those who’ve never won the big one.</p><h3><b>Most overlooked coach: Tom Livatino, Loyola</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Only true high school hoops junkies are likely to know the Ramblers have averaged 23 victories a year in their last 13 full seasons under Livatino. They’ve picked up eight regional titles in that time, as well as a sectional title in 2014. Their 30-4 team in 2019-20, arguably Livatino’s best, was set to play for a sectional title before the COVID-19 pandemic shut every-thing down. Livatino also averaged 20 wins a season in five seasons at Lincoln Park, where the Lions won three regional titles.</p><p>Still, perhaps the strongest indicator of Livatino’s impact is that opponents hate the tough, defensive-minded grind they have to deal with when playing Loyola.</p><h3><b>Most consistent head coach: Mike Oliver, Curie</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Oliver has built quite the résumé with the Condors, leading them to a Class 4A title in 2016 and three city championships, the last in 2024. Although many of their achievements aren’t appreciated enough outside the city, the long history of success can’t be denied. Perhaps no coach in the state has won as consistently for as long as Oliver has, building a<br>578-176 record in 30-plus years. It isn’t just about the win totals, either — the consistency also applies to his style and approach, the type of players on his teams and the expectations of his program.</p><h3><b>Most underrated coach: Eric Millstone</b></h3><h3></h3><p>There were some lean years after Millstone first started at Palatine, but he has quietly and clearly put his stamp on the program over 18 seasons by instilling discipline, maximizing talent and implementing a defensive scheme that has transformed the Pirates into an effective force.</p><p>Over the last five seasons, Palatine has averaged 24 wins. They had a breakthrough in 2024 with an appearance in Champaign, where they finished fourth in the state tournament in Class 4A. They also won a school-record 29 games last season.</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks beat Blues for first win after Patrick Kane's dramatic entrance
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> debuted a new team intro video Tuesday. Five minutes later, they debuted another new intro video — just for Patrick Kane.</p><p>It was an over-the-top welcome back to Chicago for Kane, complete with massive No. 88 numbers wheeled onto the United Center ice. But perhaps it was rightly dramatic, given the anticipation for the moment. </p><p>The Hawks built upon the sellout crowd's energy with a much-improved and much-needed team effort, beating the Blues 4-2 to earn their first victory of the season.</p><p>"Getting ready to go out for the introduction was definitely a little emotional," Kane said. "You're skating off the ice and it's surreal, because [you] didn't know if you'd have that chance to do it again. So it's pretty special."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Blackhawks really went all out for Patrick Kane’s reintroduction to Chicago: <a href="https://t.co/NxNZYNvhU6">pic.twitter.com/NxNZYNvhU6</a></p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCST/status/2107625412507709843?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 7, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Kane individually had a quiet night despite skating nearly 21 minutes. He had no points and two shots on goal. His five-year-old son Trick will be satisfied with the result alone, though, and so will his dad.</p><p>"Having him around and knowing what's going on, aware of everything, it makes it that much more special," Kane said. "He was really stressed out the past few days with us being 0-3. He's checking the standings and looking at everything already. He'll be happy we got a win tonight."</p><p>Artyom Levshunov made an incredible play to set up Anton Frondell's go-ahead goal in the second period, and the Hawks' defense as a whole had tighter gaps and more active sticks. Goalie Spencer Knight was stellar, too, making 26 saves.</p><p>"For us to be a really good team, we have to be on top of people and we have to play fast," coach Jeff Blashill said. "We have to keep building on that."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">An extremely bright flash of potential from Artyom Levshunov: <a href="https://t.co/6ky6KX0iTv">pic.twitter.com/6ky6KX0iTv</a></p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCST/status/2107646024450032094?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 7, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Special guests</b></h3><p>Beloved former players Jonathan Toews, Niklas Hjalmarsson and Eddie Olczyk — who just retired from his Kraken broadcasting duties to focus solely on NHL on TNT broadcasts — were in the building for Kane's big night.</p><p>Many of the Hawks' young players got to meet them for the first time Tuesday morning. Toews stood on the bench during morning skate, chatting with Connor Bedard — who participated in the first half of skate again. Afterward, Toews shook hands with Oliver Moore and Nick Lardis in the locker room.</p><p>Hjalmarsson brought his two sons, Theo and Oliver, who collected autographs all around the room. They ended up in a long conversation — in Swedish, of course — with Frondell.</p><h3><b>Forward needed</b></h3><p>Teuvo Teravainen suffered an apparent ankle or knee injury during the second period and won't play Thursday at the Islanders, Blashill said.</p><p>With Andrew Mangiapane considered week-to-week with his lower-body injury, the Hawks will need to call up another forward.</p>

entries.title: Young Blackhawks learning how to maintain confidence through bad games: 'You're not a loser'
entries.summary: <p>Young <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> forward Oliver Moore was watching YouTube on Sunday, decompressing after the Hawks' tiring and frustrating opening road trip, when he stumbled upon a video of Boston Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla.</p><p>Mazzulla's message in the video struck a chord in Moore's brain. After practice Monday, the 21-year-old Minnesotan was still thinking about it.</p><p>"He was talking about [how] when you're losing, you're not a loser," Moore said. "We're not identified by our losses; we're identified by our process. Even if we're winning, we're not winners. We're here to get better, and we're here to stay motivated.</p><p>"The challenge is, if you lose a game, coming in and acting the same way, being the same person. And if you're winning, [the challenge is] the same. You always want to identify how you can get better, no matter what. And we have time to do that now."</p><p>Moore added in that last comment himself, and he's right: the Hawks still have almost an entire season — 80 out of 84 games — ahead of them to figure out how to get better. They finally <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/06/blackhawks-blues-first-win-patrick-kane-entrance" >slid a win</a> under their belts Tuesday, too.</p><p>He and most of his teammates are at ages when development can happen quickly and suddenly. They have the talent necessary to become solid NHL players, too.</p><p>But one of the most difficult elements of developing at the pro level is navigating the inevitably frequent failures that occur along the bumpy ride. If that discourages you, you might never reach your potential, regardless of talent.</p><p>Most NHL franchises try to avoid completely bottoming out in the standings for that reason. The Hawks, however, have spent years in the basement while accumulating all of these talented youngsters.</p><p>Most franchises also keep plenty of veterans around to insulate and guide their kids. The Hawks, however, have almost entirely turned their roster over to youth.</p><p>For the Hawks to take a large step forward this season — and their rough first week revealed that step will need to be large indeed — the kids will have to collectively maintain confidence with aplomb, even through bad plays, bad shifts, bad periods and bad games.</p><p>Understandably, player confidence is something Hawks coach Jeff Blashill is monitoring closely. He was heartened that the opening trip seemingly didn't dent it too much.</p><p>Blashill gives three pieces of advice. The first: "Control what you can control." The second: "Focus on the process" more than on results. And the third: "Have fun."</p><p>"You only get a chance to do this for so long, and you better enjoy it," Blashill said. Watching Journey perform at the United Center on Monday reminded him that hockey players, unlike rock stars, don't get to do what they love for their entire lives.</p><div class="Enhancement" rattled by setbacks and demotions — such as Rinzel's healthy scratch Saturday against the Sabres — than they used to.</p><p>"For anybody, when you're playing at your best, you're confident and not really thinking about, 'What's going to happen if I don't make this play?'" Vlasic said during training camp.</p><p>"There were a couple points in the season last year where...I'd have a couple bad games [with] a couple turnovers, a couple goals [against], and then I'm in my head, I'm not playing at that same level of confidence. This year, if something bad happens, it's in one ear, out the other."</p><p>What does it take psychologically to operate like that? Fellow defenseman Wyatt Kaiser, who probably could've been a philosopher in another life, explains it better than anyone.</p><p>The speed of hockey and the frequency of shifts makes it relatively easy to move on from one bad play, Kaiser explains. You don't have much time to dwell on it before hopping over the boards again. </p><p>It's more difficult, though, to compartmentalize an entirely bad game, especially at home that night.</p><p>"You have time to sit there and think about it, right?" said Kaiser, 24. "Sometimes you feel so much pressure [because] this is all that's going on in your life. Maybe not all that's going on, but it's very important, and you want to be good.</p><p>"To be honest, you kind of put into perspective: 'OK, it's a long season. Everybody's going to make mistakes. It doesn't matter who you are. The best players are going to have bad games.' And also [you know] that doesn't make you a bad player."</p><p>The next morning, he shifts to a forward-looking mindset: reviewing video, recognizing mistakes and designing specific, actionable adjustments to avoid making the same mistakes again.</p><p>"You remember that it's never going to be easy," Kaiser added. "If you're trying to be the best and trying to perform at the highest level, it is never going to be easy. You're going to have to go through the process, and the process is <i>hard.</i></p><p>"You go out every night with a chance you're going to fail or succeed. There's not really an in-between. ... And it's human nature: you're going to fail, you're going to get knocked down. To be able to get back up and continue to put yourself out there and have confidence in yourself is a true winner."</p>

entries.title: 3 shot at West Pullman gas station overnight
entries.summary: <p>Three people were wounded in a shooting early Wednesday at a gas station in West Pullman on the Far South Side. </p><p>Around 1:30 a.m., three people — 17, 18 and 24, were at the gas station in the 11600 block of South Michigan Avenue when a black SUV pulled up and someone inside opened fire, Chicago police said. </p><p>The 18-year-old was shot in the shoulder, the 17-year-old in the torso and the 24-year-old in the ankle, police said. </p><p>All three were taken to Roseland Hospital by a white vehicle where they were in fair condition, officials said. </p><p>Area 2 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Wildfire smoke preparedness is essential to protect most vulnerable Chicagoans
entries.summary: <p>As a child growing up in New York City in the 1990s, I remember trudging through nearly a foot of snow to get to public school, which almost never closed. Each time, city crews ensured that the roads and sidewalks were salted in advance. A fleet of snowplows quickly cleared streets so that buses could run. The preparations were not only at the city level; for their part, parents and caregivers bundled up their children in gloves, hats, winter coats and mittens to brave the cold. Community groups held winter coat drives for those who could not afford them.</p><p>Thirty years later, my childhood self could not have predicted that U.S. cities in the Northeast and Midwest would be facing a very different variety of recurring extreme weather event: wildfire smoke transported from Canada — a threat that has hit Chicago particularly hard in recent years and won’t be disappearing anytime soon.</p><p>Amid the myriad weather predictions worldwide related to 2026-2027 super El Nino conditions, the Canadian government has released a <a class="Link" href="https://climatedata.ca/news/what-the-developing-exceptional-el-nino-means-for-canada-in-2026-27/" target="_blank" >report predicting an uptick in wildfires</a> across multiple regions in spring and summer 2027.</p><p>Looking back at the last several summers, it’s hard to identify one where Chicago was not affected by transported wildfire smoke. In June 2023, Chicago’s air quality was at the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2023/06/27/chicagos-air-quality-were-in-the-crosshairs-wildfires-and-wind-push-regions-air-to-worst-in-the-world-global-pollution-index-shows/" target="_blank" >bottom of the list of cities</a> worldwide.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-360000" name="module-360000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>And while the smoke filled the air across the city, its dangers impacted some communities more than others.</p><p>In a <a class="Link" href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41370-026-00956-6" target="_blank" >newly published study</a>, our team of investigators at the <a class="Link" href="https://globalhealth.duke.edu/" target="_blank" >Duke Global Health Institute </a>and the <a class="Link" href="https://ceche.uic.edu/" target="_blank" >University of Illinois Chicago Center for Extreme Conditions and Health Excellence</a> examined patterns of exposure across the city during the June 2023 wildfire smoke event. While we found that no neighborhood was untouched by elevated levels of particulate matter, neighborhoods with worse baseline air quality, lower socioeconomic status and higher proportions of non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic populations took a longer time to recover in the days after the event, further amplifying existing air quality exposure disparities.</p><p>Poor air quality is linked to many adverse health outcomes, including respiratory disease, cardiometabolic disease and cancer. The exposure risks are even larger for vulnerable populations, including older adults, children and those with preexisting conditions such as asthma or diabetes. A 2026 <a class="Link" href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12871454/" target="_blank" >study in Science Advances</a> found that wildfire smoke particles <sub> </sub>accounted for more than 24,000 annual deaths in the U.S. between 2006 and 2020.</p><p>In July, the city of Chicago once again ranked among the worst in air quality in the world, with a composite daily <a class="Link" href="https://www.airnow.gov/state/?name=illinois" target="_blank" >Air Quality Index for fine particulate matter of 400</a>. For a U.S. city to reach an Air Quality Index above 300 — classified as “hazardous” — is historically highly unusual.</p><p>Given that wildfire smoke is not going away, this is a public health problem that even regions of the U.S. historically unaffected by wildfires must be prepared for, especially during the summer months when heat plays a role in the equation. Early warning systems are needed to reduce exposure to vulnerable populations. Just as Northeastern and Midwestern municipalities provide alerts and cleared roadways in a snowstorm in the winter months, it should be regular practice to share air quality alerts and provide access to <a class="Link" href="https://www.epa.gov/emergencies-iaq/wildfires-and-indoor-air-quality-iaq" target="_blank" >mitigation tools during a wildfire event</a> in the summer.</p><p>Such strategies might include, but are not limited to, indoor air sensors, N95 and KN95 masks and portable air cleaners with a HEPA air filter. For older housing without central air conditioning, at-risk individuals should have affordable access to fans and air conditioners so that they do not have to choose between thermal comfort and breathing smoke through an open window.</p><p>Looking back on this summer’s transported wildfire smoke events and the pattern over the last several summers, <a class="Link" href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cwyq93j34lgo" target="_blank" >some have suggested</a> that Canada should do more to prevent and address wildfires so that their impact does not reach the U.S. This would not change the reality that extreme weather events are increasing in frequency and severity. Today, firefighters continue to battle against fires in Yosemite, with <a class="Link" href="https://www.fire.ca.gov/incidents/2026/9/15/dome-fire" target="_blank" >only 40% contained</a> so far. Regardless of the source of the smoke, we must take responsibility for extreme weather events which affect the health of the most at-risk populations here in the U.S.</p><p>As wildfire smoke events become the norm even for areas geographically distant from the source, U.S. cities need to prepare with the same practiced vigilance they apply to snowstorms, and the time to prepare is now — not after the smoke and its attendant damage have arrived.</p><p><i>Melissa Fiffer is a senior research scientist at the University of Illinois Chicago's </i><a class="Link" href="https://cehi.uic.edu/" target="_blank" ><i>Children’s Environmental Health Initiative</i></a><i>, adjunct assistant professor at UIC's School of Public Health and co-director of the </i><a class="Link" href="https://ceche.uic.edu/" target="_blank" ><i>UIC Center for Extreme Conditions and Health Excellence</i></a><i> Data Core. She is also a University of Illinois Public Voices fellow with The OpEd Project.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-220000" name="module-220000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Death penalty should be killed nationwide
entries.summary: <p>There are 23 states that have abolished the death penalty. Now Tennessee has <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/10/02/nx-s1-5987954/tennessee-governor-pauses-executions-after-christa-pike-survives-2-lethal-injections" target="_blank" >paused</a> all executions for the remainder of 2026. That decision comes after yet another botched execution attempt (of Christa Pike) using intravenous injection.</p><p>One traditional line of thought is that ultimate judgment belongs to a higher power. The other approach is that we infallible humans have constructed a legal system so failure-proof that the state should have the right to kill its citizens.</p><p>That supposed infallibility is contradicted by the constant stream of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/12/6/23989776/chicago-taxpayers-nearly-700-million-lawsuits-framed-police" >cases being overturned</a> in our courts. Of the thousands of executions carried out in the last century, there were certainly some done in error. How do you justify even one mistake? Is there a formula for that? And there is no convincing evidence the death penalty is a deterrent.</p><p>The average gap between commission of a crime and executions is<a class="Link" href="https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/death-row/death-row-time-on-death-row" target="_blank" > 22-23 years</a><i>.</i> People spend decades in prison wondering if and when they will be executed. How is that not cruel and unusual punishment? Prison is supposed to be punishment, not deliberate torture.</p><p>Killing someone under the total control of the state is immoral and is itself murder.</p><p>Each of the five methods of execution used in this country is barbaric in its own way. Four of the five have measurable failure rates, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/executions/botched-executions" target="_blank" >Death Penalty Information Center.</a> The supposedly humane lethal injection method has the highest botched execution rate. </p><p>End the death penalty, I say. </p><p>Those whose crimes are so unforgivable or those who are a threat to society can be sentenced to life without parole. In the case of wrongful convictions, sentences can be commuted, people can be pardoned and seek redress and can be released. The wrongly executed cannot be released from the grave.</p><p><i>Michael Hart, West Ridge</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-df0000" name="module-df0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Avalon Regal needs a sound check </h3><p>I agree with Sun-Times architecture columnist Lee Bey that the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/10/02/historic-avalon-regal-theater-play-250000-repair-funds" >Avalon Regal Theater</a> is a beautiful building. But its very muddy acoustics are a serious flaw. At the Avalon Regal, I once had great difficulty understanding the dialogue of a well-attended and well-produced play by August Wilson.</p><p>I suggest that the city of Chicago and private foundations pause to do a thorough acoustic remediation analysis before committing scarce funds to save the Avalon Regal. Any such analysis should include testing a new sound system with a full house. All auditoriums sound different, and usually better with an audience of echo-muffling human bodies.</p><p><i>A. Christopher Wilson, West Rogers Park</i></p><h3>Ride toward success </h3><p>I will add one more critical missing item to Sun-Times columnist Neil Steinberg's assertion that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/10/04/public-toilet-chicago-bathroom-desert-paris-london-tourism-steinberg" target="_blank" >lack of public toilets</a> keep Chicago from being a world-class city.</p><p>The absence of express transit service from <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/mayor/press_room/press_releases/2026/april/ohare-worlds-busiest.html" target="_blank" >America’s busiest airport</a> — O'Hare — to the central business/tourism district is a glaring gap in Chicago's world class resume!"</p><p><i>Kirk Dillard, former chair, Regional Transportation Authority</i></p><h3>Waste of time</h3><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/6128990-john-kennedy-donald-trump-tom-cotton-phone-number-share-criticism/" target="_blank" >fight</a> between President Donald Trump and Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., over permanent daylight saving time is a tempest in a teapot. Trump decries the effort involved in changing clocks twice a year. Cotton points out that with year-round daylight saving time, children’s safety and health are jeopardized in the winter by having to wait in the dark for a school bus. Safety seems a better argument than convenience.</p><p>The idea that the effort to change two to five clocks twice a year is too much for anyone to bear is ridiculous. Leave it alone. Concentrate rather on more important matters, such as rising gas prices, increased costs of healthcare, difficulties in securing a mortgage, and above all, the ongoing war with Iran. That’s where Congress and the president should be paying attention.</p><p><i>Frank L. Schneider, East Lake View</i></p><h3>Schmitt’s failure to apologize is Trumplike</h3><p>It's quite ironic that the very day stories appear about Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., possibly being JD Vance’s running mate in 2028, he embarrasses himself by calling former special counsel Jack Smith a “dirtbag” while presenting <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/10/02/eric-schmitts-hawk-hawkeyes-jack-smith-donald-trump-republicans-s-e-cupp" >false evidence confusing</a> the Atlanta Hawks and the Iowa Hawkeyes. Hey, any of us could have made that mistake. But almost all of us would have apologized. But not Schmitt. He’s learned from the best liar of all. Never admit a mistake — even when you put in power those who have the audacity to disagree with you. Never apologize. Never look embarrassed.</p><p>Forget about the No. 2 spot, senator. Throw your hat in the ring for president. You are eminently qualified. Perhaps your title could be changed to what you hung on Smith.</p><p><i>Kevin Coughlin, Evanston</i></p><h3>Thank you, White Sox </h3><p>What joy for this longtime Sox fan since the days of Chico Carrasquel, Nellie Fox and Minnie Minoso. Happiness reigns. The spirit and success of the present squad is contagious. For a moment we can put aside Iran, Gaza, inflation and our president trying to make Washington, D.C., look like the Wisconsin Dells.</p><p><i>Philip S. Witt, Northbrook</i></p><h3>How about this stadium shuffle? </h3><p>It just seems like Illinois and Indiana politicians can't come up with answers. It might make sense to put the Sox next to the Fire stadium on Roosevelt Road and maybe put the Bear's on 87th Street and DuSable Lake Shore Drive or knock down Rate Field and build the Bears stadium there. And if it's state funded, it may save a lot of money. Now the fumble is recovered.</p><p><i>Joseph Battaglia, Clearing</i></p><h3>Bears: Look north at NU</h3><p>I hope everyone in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> management is paying attention to Northwestern University, which just proved with its new<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports/2026/10/02/fans-get-first-official-look-at-northwesterns-long-awaited-new-ryan-field" > Ryan Field</a> that it is possible to build a new stadium in the Chicago area.</p><p><i>Steven Herr, West Ridge</i><br></p>

entries.title: As a proud Italian American, I can't get behind the Christopher Columbus adoration
entries.summary: <p>As an Italian American in Chicago, I’ve loved celebrating my heritage in so many ways — going to <a class="Link" href="https://damatoschicago.com/" target="_blank" >D’Amatos</a> to get cannolis for Sunday family dinner; gathering with fellow paisans at the Taylor Street Little Italy Festa; playing tombola (Italian bingo) at the <a class="Link" href="https://www.mariasslauretana.com/" target="_blank" >Maria SS Lauretana Society</a> on the Northwest Side. And yes, even mourning the death of stalwart spots like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-history/2026/05/23/closed-chicago-businesses-miss-most-what-you-told-us" target="_blank" >Sabatino’s</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://franoi.com/dining/anna-maria-pasteria-closes-up-shop/" target="_blank" >Anna Maria Pasteria</a>, RIP.</p><p>But one Italian American celebration I cannot get behind is the ongoing adoration of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/10/13/columbus-day-parade-state-street" >Christopher Columbus</a>.</p><p>For years, we’ve been told the controversial explorer was some kind of hero to rest our green-white-and-red laurels on, that he was the prime example of Genoan stock who sailed the ocean blue in 1492 and discovered America, giving us Italians a sense of ownership in the country’s very origins. But that lie is as much a fraud as the man himself.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fc0000" name="module-fc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Columbus actually never stepped foot on the North American mainland (<a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/answer-sheet/wp/2013/10/14/christopher-columbus-3-things-you-think-he-did-that-he-didnt/" target="_blank" >Oct. 12 </a>is when he arrived at the Bahamas), and somehow over time we’ve just accepted the blatant omission that Indigenous peoples were already living on American soil and creating real communities that would have an ongoing influence on the country (lest we forget where the words Chicago and Milwaukee come from). That’s just the soft truth, though. The other is the dark web of oppression Columbus and his cronies inflicted on the <a class="Link" href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/who-were-taino-original-inhabitants-columbus-island-73824867/" target="_blank" >Taino people</a> in the island territories he commanded, enslaving them and inflicting enforced labor, brutal violence and mutilation and the introduction of infectious diseases that threatened to wipe out the population.</p><p>Is this who Italian Americans really want as a representative?</p><p>I’d be the first to stand on the hill of needing strong examples of Italian pride in this country — after the decades of ridicule and racist taunts lodged at early Italian immigrants. Rewriting that history and edifying Italian contributions to art, culture, business and overall society is sorely needed. We still live in a time that two-dimensional characters of Italian culture are kept alive by mob bosses and families like the Corleones and Sopranos. I shake my head every time I see a new bottle of whiskey laid at the grave of Al Capone, who’s buried near my great-grandmother Mary at Mount Carmel Catholic Cemetery in Hillside. But continuing to elevate Columbus as some kind of antithesis to “The Godfather” stereotype is a big bunch of gabagool. Knowing his reign of terror, wasn’t Columbus the biggest mob boss of all?</p><p>I’m proud to celebrate Italian American Heritage and Culture Month every October and see new developments like the Italian Cultural Institute in Chicago, which just moved to a larger space at 150 N. Michigan Ave., or the opening of the <a class="Link" href="https://chgoitalmuseum.com/" target="_blank" >Florence Scala Italian American Museum</a> in Little Italy, just blocks away from where my own grandparents were married at the former St. Callistus Roman Catholic Church. But my excitement changed when I heard museum owners and leaders with the Joint Civic Committee of Italian Americans claim “victory” with the reclamation of the oft-vandalized Columbus statue that was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2020/7/31/21349346/chicago-removes-last-christopher-columbus-statue-far-south-side" >removed</a> from Arrigo Park during the pandemic. With plans to display it in the museum, they’ve <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2026/08/14/museum-that-will-house-little-italys-columbus-statue-readies-for-opening-as-taylor-st-fest-kicks-off/" target="_blank" >said</a> in recent statements that it represents an “icon of faith and hope for our ethnic group.”</p><p>But they don’t speak for all of us.</p><h3>Replace Columbus </h3><p>When Joe Biden issued the first-ever presidential <a class="Link" href="https://mx.usembassy.gov/a-proclamation-on-indigenous-peoples-day-2021/" target="_blank" >proclamation</a> for Indigenous Peoples' Day in 2021, it felt like real progress to honor those who are our true American pioneers. As a little girl, I was taught to have a great amount of respect for Native Americans. My Evanston grandparents uprooted to Los Alamos, New Mexico, in the 1940s to work on the Manhattan Project where they befriended members of the native Pueblo community and taught their children and grandchildren to honor America’s first citizens. If an American president can change course on what we celebrate every second Monday of October, why can’t we in Chicago, a city where Native contributions are embedded into the very fabric of our streets? If you’ve wondered who came up with the genius idea to create diagonal pathways like Archer and Milwaukee avenues to get across the city quicker, well you can thank Native Americans for that — those are their old trails.</p><p>So, yes, let’s keep the parade and October as our pride month, but it’s time for Italian Americans to get a new hero behind them. It’s not like there aren’t plenty to choose from — Dante, Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Galileo and Maria Montessori come to mind.</p><p>In Chicago we even have an incredibly worthy option with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/02/18/arrigo-parks-columbus-statue-saint-frances-xavier-cabrini" >Mother Frances Xavier Cabrini</a>, who will soon have her own statue erected in the spot Columbus vacated in Arrigo Park. Cabrini is recognized as a saint and was the first U.S. citizen to be canonized by the Catholic Church for her work, largely helping, well, immigrants. She was behind the establishment of schools, hospitals and orphanages from the time she arrived in New York to her final years in Chicago, where she opened the Near North Side Assumption School and the former (sigh) Columbus Hospital in Lake View. On Oct. 12, I’d encourage my fellow Italian Americans to pass on saluting Columbus and instead pay a visit to Lake View’s <a class="Link" href="https://cabrininationalshrine.org/" target="_blank" >National Shrine of St. Frances Xavier Cabrini</a> and honor one our own who actually did great things for this country and this city.</p><p><i>Selena Fragassi is a Chicago area music journalist who often writes for the Sun-Times.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1b0000" name="module-1b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Parent's worst fear becomes recurring nightmare
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My two youngest children have special needs. Both have the mentality of a 7- or 8-year-old. Today, my daughter (13) told the school counselor that her brother (15) has been touching her inappropriately. I feel like I'm reliving a nightmare. Six years ago, my oldest son touched her. He was charged and tried as an adult.</p><p>My daughter is now staying with my mother-in-law until both kids can get counseling. I don't know what to do or how to act. I don't even know why I'm writing you. I guess I just need to get it off my chest. How do I survive this a second time? — <i>HEARTBROKEN IN MISSOURI</i></p><p><b>DEAR HEARTBROKEN:</b> Please accept my sympathy. You were smart to get your daughter out of the house to a place that is safe and where she is loved. This is a heavy load for any parent to carry, and because you have made no mention of a spouse, I assume you are doing it alone. You said your children will be getting counseling, and I think it would be a good idea for you to get some for yourself as well until you regain your balance.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I have three kids, ages 2 to 7. Most of his siblings' kids are old enough to look after themselves. My sisters-in-law love ladies' day getaways and brag about the "family togetherness" they maintain.</p><p>While I enjoy occasional outings, I'm less outgoing, and my batteries recharge at home. Sometimes, these events are more of a drain physically and emotionally than they are worth to me, not to mention that the destination is rarely of any interest to me. So far, I've obliged just to keep them happy, at my own and my family's expense.</p><p>My problem is that they've started doing these once a month. The next destination is over three hours away, meaning I'd have to get my kids up at 5 a.m., get a babysitter and make arrangements for their separate school transportation. When I cram my schedule so full, I end up tired, stressed and sometimes sick.</p><p>I love my in-laws, and they say my presence is important to them. I've already said no to this outing, but I'm still being pressured. My husband supports my decision either way. Taking off work is not an option for him.</p><p>Am I just being selfish if I don't go? Their happiness depends on my choice. — <i>INDIANA IN-LAW</i></p><p><b>DEAR IN-LAW:</b> Their happiness does not depend on your choice. If it did, they would be more considerate of your situation when setting up these excursions. If they continue to pressure you, tell them all the reasons why it's so burdensome for you to join them. As moms with slightly older kids, they should understand where you're coming from, and they may even have some ideas to help make it less of a hassle. Of course, if you simply don't want to go, all you can do is keep saying no until they get the message.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: The new Trattoria Lo So aims to be Monteverde’s ‘cool aunt’

had.”</p><p>She “wears a kaftan and smokes a long cigarette” and has heaps of confidence, Grueneberg said, comparing the new spot to her prominent West Loop Italian restaurant known for its class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In addition to seafood and vegetable dishes prepared over a robata-style grill (an open-hearth grill typically used in Japanese cooking), Lo So’s menu will include some Monteverde personality with fresh pastas cooked in the wood-fired oven, Grueneberg (left) and Sullivan said.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“When you make [dishes] with dry pasta, it's like you're allowed to undercook it in the water and finish cooking in the sauce,” she continued. “That's a technique that's really challenging to do with a fresh extruded pasta, because you have to cook the flour enough to not allow it to be gummy.”</p><p>Her mentor, Tony Mantuano of the acclaimed Spaggia, where Grueneberg was promoted as executive chef in 2010, taught her that.</p><p>The one-story Bucktown space allowed the restaurateurs to install two important features: a wood-burning oven and a charcoal grill.</p><p>In addition to seafood and vegetable dishes prepared over a robata-style grill (an open-hearth grill typically used in Japanese cooking), Lo So’s menu will include some Monteverde personality with fresh pastas cooked in the wood-fired oven, Grueneberg and Sullivan said.</p><p>“Having live fuel is a challenge and an exciting thing altogether,” Grueneberg said. “That fire, that smoke, is going to tell the story of the menu there.”</p><p>The robata grill and wood-fired oven seem to be what they’re most excited about: “We always love putting different skewers on the menu,” known as “spiedini” in Italian, Sullivan said. “We'll have a lot of [those] coming off of that grill, or even things getting marked on the grill, finished in that wood-fired oven.”</p><p>Pastificio Mancini also grows the wheat it mills into flour for its pastas, which is not as common throughout Italy, Grueneberg said. “It’s the full process,” she said. The next phase of their restaurant includes an October trip to Marche, in part to see how the pasta is made.</p><p>Food has always been an important part of Sullivan’s life.</p><p>Her father is Michael Sullivan, owner of Goldyburgers in Forest Park. She went on to study the culinary arts at Kendall College, then perfected her ramen and Japanese techniques at the now-closed Yusho in Logan Square before moving on to Parachute in Avondale.</p><p>In 2016, she landed at Monteverde.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-530000" name="image-530000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/53f787c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F28%2Fd6db9c2c4f0d96106d6fcc2237d7%2Fbolognese-09xx23-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/90fca3c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F28%2Fd6db9c2c4f0d96106d6fcc2237d7%2Fbolognese-09xx23-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ec9f456/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F28%2Fd6db9c2c4f0d96106d6fcc2237d7%2Fbolognese-09xx23-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The pasta bolognese from Monteverde, located at 1020 W. Madison St. in the West Loop, is known for its contemporary takes on fresh pasta dishes, like its bolognese.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In the decade or so that <a class="Link" href="https://monteverdechicago.com/about/" target="_blank" ><u>Sullivan has been cooking at Monteverde,</u></a> she’s gained a notable amount of press and hype, including being named a finalist this year in the James Beard Awards’ Emerging Chef category. At the West Town eatery, she’s known for her “atipica” (“atypical” in Italian) style: She blends local, seasonal ingredients with culinary whimsy and Italian flair.</p><p>While the details of the rotating menu are still being worked out, Sullivan is meditating on the “feeling” they want to create for guests. The renowned duo said they “are building a restaurant that we want everyone to feel like they can eat at.”</p><p>But the possibilities are endless, Sullivan said: “Homey dishes like casseroles, baked pastas … you can go so many directions.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-460000" target="_blank" >Privacy Policy</a></p> </div> </form> </bsp-form> </div> </div><p>I first read a version of this play last summer at the Eugene O’Neill Theater Center, where I attended the National Critics Institute (Pharel was attending the National Playwrights Conference). Then, the words on the page didn’t strike me in the way they did in the mouths of actors on stage.</p><p>Perhaps that’s due to my recent check-ins with my niece, a sophomore at a large university in Texas. As an avid consumer of news, I’ve been inundated with reports from the alleged sexual assault at Cornell University — and have been subsequently compelled to have safety talks with my niece.</p><p>This play, written by Pharel, a Gen-Z Afro-Latina from Miami, poses some really big questions: Why is it that so many Black and brown girls go missing? What’s behind the teenage girl obsession with true crime? What does it say about us, as adults, that girls feel so unprotected in society?</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.5" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> “Dead Girl’s Quinceañera” </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-550000" name="module-550000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When</b>: Through Nov. 1<br><b>Where</b>: Goodman Theatre, 170 N. Dearborn St.<br><b>Info</b>: <a class="Link" href="https://www.goodmantheatre.org/show/dead-girls-quinceanera/" target="_blank" ><u>Tickets</u></a> from $29</div> </div><p>In this play, three 15ish-year-old girls try to find their missing friend Maria, who disappeared after her Quinceañera. The true beauty of this production, besides the wonderful Quinceañera gowns by costume designer Raquel Adorno, is that the language is much less preachy than my intro here. As I reflect, I feel like the old-man-on-the-front-porch worrying about the youngsters — but if this play taught me anything, it’s that the youngsters will be OK. Here, the resourceful young women are packing a pink taser that they vow to use to send a number of men “back to Jesus.”</p><p>Despite the heavy themes, this play is <i>hilarious</i>. Pharel captures the voices of teen girls with such authenticity and vigor that the 90 minutes fly by in a blur. When the show opens, it has been 19 hours since anyone has heard from Maria, and Salma (Jacqueline Guillen), a true-crime aficionado, is on the case. She recruits her besties Phoebe (Ariana Burks), who is Maria’s cousin, and Este (Carmen Berkeley) to help.</p><p>What ensues is a clever who-done-it led by these three teens who set up an HQ in their hang out spot — a shed in Salma’s backyard — complete with the classic bulletin board to track and connect clues.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6e34a31/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7591x4260+0+396/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1f%2F98%2Ffe6dcd2048d29e2f79ef374aa5ba%2F5-dead-girls-quinceanera-goodman-production-photos.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b828c63/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7591x4260+0+396/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1f%2F98%2Ffe6dcd2048d29e2f79ef374aa5ba%2F5-dead-girls-quinceanera-goodman-production-photos.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6e34a31/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7591x4260+0+396/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F1f%2F98%2Ffe6dcd2048d29e2f79ef374aa5ba%2F5-dead-girls-quinceanera-goodman-production-photos.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Playwright Phanésia Pharel captures the voices of teen girls with such authenticity and vigor that the 90 minute runtime flies by in a blur.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Justin Barbin</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The direction by Melia Bensussen, the artistic director of the National Playwrights Conference at the Eugene O'Neill Theater Center, is spot on. Bensussen, who saw early drafts of the play (she’s directing the rolling premiere which also includes a stop at Hartford Stage where she’s artistic director), gives the actors the space to not only crack the case with style, but also hash out their teenage world views along the way.</p><p>These girls discuss politics, race, religion through teenage feminist perspectives that are refreshing to hear on stage.</p><p>Some of the happenings here feel very Miami, true to the playwright’s biography. Race is not simply Black and white. Phoebe and Maria are cousins, but their conflict is in part due to Phoebe having one parent born “on the wrong side of the island,” referring to Maria being Dominican, and Phoebe having one Dominican parent and one Haitian parent. Many of us have watched from afar as Cubans in Miami were under the spotlight during Trump’s last campaign. Here, Salma often refers to her brother's political stances, at one point calling him a Proud Boy.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-320000" name="image-320000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/06c6ed6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7520x4220+0+399/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F8d%2Fa0addc744a55b70d60b7bcd8464f%2F1-dead-girls-quinceanera-goodman-production-photos.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b88b3de/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7520x4220+0+399/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F8d%2Fa0addc744a55b70d60b7bcd8464f%2F1-dead-girls-quinceanera-goodman-production-photos.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/10eb7a5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7520x4220+0+399/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F8d%2Fa0addc744a55b70d60b7bcd8464f%2F1-dead-girls-quinceanera-goodman-production-photos.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt=" Jacqueline Guillén in "Dead Girl's Quinceañera" at the Goodman Theatre. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/10eb7a5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7520x4220+0+399/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F8d%2Fa0addc744a55b70d60b7bcd8464f%2F1-dead-girls-quinceanera-goodman-production-photos.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/86ab204/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7520x4220+0+399/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F8d%2Fa0addc744a55b70d60b7bcd8464f%2F1-dead-girls-quinceanera-goodman-production-photos.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/10eb7a5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7520x4220+0+399/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbd%2F8d%2Fa0addc744a55b70d60b7bcd8464f%2F1-dead-girls-quinceanera-goodman-production-photos.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Jacqueline Guillén is an absolute force as Salma, a sharp-tongued sleuth.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Justin Barbin</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The performances here are stellar, which may be in part due to the play being a rolling world premiere, which means this cast has performed the show in full before, which usually isn’t the case when a new play comes to town. Guillen is an absolute force as Salma. She’s captivating as the over aggressive, sharp-tongued sleuth. In one scene, as she explains her strained relationship with her father, she’s elbow-dropping a bean bag chair WWE-style. Berkeley is deft as Este, the peacekeeper between the strong personalities of Salma and Phoebe. She’s in a different financial class than the group. She has a job, which Salma discovers because she often “smells like chicken.”</p><p>A lot of us are worried about the kids these days, and as the characters in this production show, rightfully so. But what we learn from this production, it’s that we as adults need to do better. But the kids will be OK, and if not, a pink taser in a purse goes a long way.</p>

entries.title: Chinatown's former 'City Hall' gets $750,000 restoration grant
entries.summary: <p>The Pui Tak Center — Chinatown's polychromatic bonanza of Chinese Eclectic architecture — has received a $750,000 grant to help restore the 98-year-old landmark.</p><p>The matching grant was announced Thursday. The center, 2216 S. Wentworth, is among 24 sites awarded grants through the Save America's Treasures program administered by the National Park Service.</p><p>It's the only Illinois project this year to receive funding from the initiative.</p><p>Pui Tak Center Executive Director David Wu said the award, along with the matching funds the group must raise, will be used to cover big-ticket items such as restoring the center's ornate windows of decorative iron and leaded glass — particularly shop windows on the first floor — and repairing the building's deteriorating roof.</p><p>Wu said a $200,000 capital grant has been set aside for the building in the state's 2027 fiscal year budget.</p><p>"We're going to try to raise the match from foundations and from individuals," he said. "So we have some work to do in terms of raising the match."</p><p>While new money awaits, preservation work on the building has been going on for at least a decade.</p><p>"We spent around $500,000 on terra cotta work and more recently, in 2022, we restored the front canopy, which is an important feature of the building," Wu said.</p><p>It cost $900,000 to restore the canopy, he said.</p><div details.</p><p>The building was designed by Christian Michaelsen and Sigurd Rognstad, two Norwegian architects who had never been to China. Central Park Ave.</p><p>"That period was still under the <a class="Link" href="https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/chinese-exclusion-act" target="_blank" >Chinese Exclusion Act</a>," Luk said. "That means during that period, there were not a lot of Chinese architects [in the U.S.] — or maybe none. And so when the On Leong association commissioned the architects to build the building, the architects were Norwegian."</p><p>Luk said Michaelsen and Rognstad did a pretty good job replicating Chinese-inspired details. But the architects sometimes got a bit off track, such as aquatic figures that resemble friendly dolphins instead of the protective, dragon-like creatures found in Chinese design.</p><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Luk said some patterns look more Greek or Roman than Chinese.</p><p>"And then the foo dogs — they look like puppies more than guardian figures," she said. "So it's very interesting about the architects thinking about trying to get it right."</p><p>The Pui Tak Center building, which houses social services, is owned by the Chinese Christian Union Church. </p><p>The church bought the building in 1993, five years after the FBI and the Chicago Police Department raided the property. Cops and agents seized the building, gambling equipment and $350,000, after learning the On Leong businessmen were operating an illegal casino there.</p><p>Wu said the church and the Pui Tak Center are working together to raise rehab and restoration funds.</p><p>He said the organizations are looking to have much of the work completed by the building's 100th anniversary in 2028.</p><p>The center has been listed on the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2025/05/07/chinatown-on-leong-merchant-association-building-pui-tak-center-national-register" target="_blank" >National Register of Historic Places</a> since 2025 and has been Chinatown's only protected city landmark since 1993.</p><p>The National Park Service said it awarded <a class="Link" href="https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/nps-awards-$24-4-million-in-save-america-s-treasures-grants.htm" target="_blank" >$24.4 million</a> in the latest round of Save America's Treasures grants. Founded in 1998, the program is funded by revenue from federal oil and gas leases.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2025/05/07/chinatown-on-leong-merchant-association-building-pui-tak-center-national-register" >Chinatown’s ‘City Hall,’ seized by feds years ago, might make National Register of Historic Places</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: ‘Rivalry is our last name:’ Chicago and Detroit battle on the dancefloor
entries.summary: <p>Memorial Day weekend 2000: Bill Clinton was in his second presidential term, the Sony Playstation II had just been released and Eminem had just dropped the fastest-selling rap album of all time. But that weekend, Detroit experienced another pivotal moment in music history: the inaugural Detroit Electronic Music Festival.</p><p>Chris Gerben fondly remembers working at that first festival. The music was “a soundtrack of early adolescence.” He went to underground raves in Detroit and nearby Windsor, Ontario.</p><p>Almost a million techno heads from across the world converged on Hart Plaza for the free, three-day event, which was the first of its kind in the Midwest.</p><p>DJs of Chicago house and Detroit techno alike say DEMF was a major sign that their homegrown, fast-paced dance music had taken the world by storm.</p><p>For the last eight years, Gerben has been living in Chicago, where he’s gotten to appreciate how important house music was in shaping electronic dance music too.</p><p>This got him wondering about the parallel origins of Detroit techno and Chicago house. Is there a rivalry between the two?</p><p>By the 1990s, both musical genres became the soundtrack to each city's signature footwork dance style, important to the culture in Chicago and Detroit. At the very least, there was a perceived rivalry in the music and the dance, and it all started with a death.</p><h3><b>Disco dies in Chicago</b></h3><p>In 1979, after Game 1 of a doubleheader between the Chicago White Sox and the Detroit Tigers at Chicago’s Comiskey Park, the Sox hosted a “<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/the-rundown-chicago-news-podcast/2024/07/22/how-house-music-found-its-roots-in-disco-dj-lady-d-on-40-years-of-the-genre" target="_blank" ><u>Disco Demolition</u></a>” event. Local DJ Steve Dahl detonated a crate of disco records in center field. Fans rushed onto the field and the night ended in a riot. Disco was declared dead.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-0b0000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>POLICE SWEEP THE FIELD WHILE A FIRE BURNS IN CENTER FIELD. THIS WAS THE SCENE AT DISCO DEMOLITION NIGHT AT COMISKEY PARK IN 1979.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jack Lenahan/Chicago Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But out of the ashes, DJs created something new. In Detroit, it was techno; in Chicago, it was house.</p><p>The late Frankie Knuckles is considered “the godfather” of Chicago house music, an upbeat, soulful blend of electronic drum machine beats and lyrical disco samples. He was instrumental in developing and popularizing this new sound in the late 1970s at the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/curious-city/2019/01/12/what-was-it-like-to-dance-at-the-warehouse-club-in-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>Warehouse Club</u></a>, a prominent dance venue where DJs remixed disco, funk and post-punk music into long, continuous tracks. At the time, it was just called “dance music.”</p><p>“When we found electronic instruments like the rolling drum machines and the sonic samplers … all of those tools allowed us to continue and to expand our creativity,” said Chicago House DJ Chip Eberhart, known as “Chip E.”</p><p>Unlike Disco, it wasn’t played on the radio. People mainly heard it during DJ sets at the Warehouse, which some people called “the House.” Some say this shorthand is where the genre’s name originated.</p><p>The DJs who recorded their sets sold them at shops, like Imports Etc. in Chicago’s Printers Row, where a young Chip E. happened to work.</p><p>“We found that if we put a sign next to a record that said ‘As Heard at the House,’ people would instantly flock to that section,” he said. “So I decided I’m gonna use that term.”</p><p>Chip E. said he and his crew — Kurt Landrum, Joe Smooth and Eric "E.T." Taylor — were intentional about branding the genre. He said they<b> </b>created the first house music EP, “Jack Trax,” and a song on that record was called simply “It’s House.”</p><p>“I made that specifically because I want to tell people this is something new, and I wanted it to be highly memorable,” he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Chip Eberhart</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>“Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit”</b></h3><p>At the same time, another disco derivative was born in metro Detroit. Techno was a futuristic, machine-driven blend of synthesizer pop, funk and disco with few lyrics, if any.</p><p>In the 1970s, DJs Juan Atkins, Kevin Saunderson and Derek May met in Belleville, roughly 30 miles west of Detroit. They formed a group called the Belleville Three and created some of the first techno tracks, including Juan Atkins’ pioneering single “No UFOs.”</p><p></p><p>At the time, techno was often referred to as “progressive music” and “Detroit house.” People mainly listened to it at clubs, warehouse raves and underground parties.</p><p>Charles “The Electrifying Mojo” Johnson brought this new sound to Detroit radio waves on his show “The Midnight Funk Association.” He and local DJ Jeff “The Wizard” Mills were instrumental in creating a community around it.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>From left to right, back to front: Derrick May, Kevin Saunderson, Blake Baxter, Eddie Fowlkes, Juan Atkins and Santonio Echols.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Norman Anderson</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In 1988, British record collector Neil Rushton released the compilation “Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit,” officially stamping a label on the genre.</p><p>Many have tried to pit house and techno against each other. But Chip E. said it wasn’t a rivalry.</p><p>“It was really more of a love fest: We loved what they did, they loved what we did,” he said. “We weren’t competing so that we would be the best. We were really competing for the dance floor. We were competing to make people move their bodies.”</p><p>There is no rivalry between the DJs, but the dance floor is a different story.</p><h3><b>Chicago footwork vs. Detroit jit</b></h3><p>House and techno became a soundtrack for Chicago footwork and Detroit jit. Both styles focus on energetic lower-body dance moves, along with arm and upper-body techniques. Creativity is key: Dancers incorporate other street dances, like ticking and hip-rolling. Chicago footwork features lightning-fast kicks, steps and turns. Detroit jit incorporates that rapid footwork, plus acrobatics and floor work, similar to breakdancing.</p><p>Detroit jit began in the 1970s, where four early dance groups shaped it. The Jitterbugs (not associated with swing dance) helped coin the dance name, and they contributed basic steps and acrobatic moves. A street gang called the Errol Flynns popularized hand moves that became known as flagging. The Funketeers from the nearby town of Inkster helped integrate popping and locking. And the most influential group, the Mad Dancers, standardized the dance form and ushered it into its current era of dynamic, fast-paced moves.</p><p>In 1980s Chicago, South Side house music dance crews, like House-O-Matic, were inspired by innovative moves from the West Side. Elvis “Bo Dollar” Chatman developed a move called the “Holy Ghost” that featured jerky body movements reminiscent of zealous worshippers in church. House-O-Matic created its own version by adding side-to-side movements. In the 1990s, RP Boo developed music that accompanied footwork battles.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a
