entries.title: White Sox set lineup for Game 3 of ALDS against Guardians
entries.summary: <p>Counting the playoffs and their plans for Game 3 of the American League Division Series, the White Sox are primed to use an opener for the 35th time in 2026 on Wednesday when they hand the ball to left-handed reliever Sean Newcomb, with the chance to clinch a postseason series at home for the first time in 120 years.</p><p>“Just the same old getting in there, getting a couple innings in, two innings in and handing it off to the next guy,” said Newcomb, in the tune of someone recounting their morning wake-up routine.</p><p>White Sox manager Will Venable intimated that after four postseason games of concentrating their innings with a fairly small group of high-leverage relievers and Sean Burke, that some pitchers who have yet to see postseason action will factor into Game 3. That suggests playoff debuts for Davis Martin and Noah Schultz as possibilities, but MLB managers aren’t paid to reveal their playoff pitching strategies hours before the games start.</p><p>“We're going to be kind of reading and reacting on this one,” Venable said. “There's a different calculus here, obviously, with a game potentially tomorrow, with no more off days, with what we've used of guys.”</p><p>The Guardians are running out a similarly lefty-heavy lineup to Game 2, where they anticipated a lot of Burke behind opener Anthony Kay.</p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-b07b91d0-c270-11f1-a685-419dc6d789f3" start="1"><li>Steven Kwan, CF (L)</li><li>Jose Ramirez, 3B (S)</li><li>Chase DeLauter, RF (L)</li><li>Jo Adell, DH (R)</li><li>Nathaniel Lowe, 1B (L)</li><li>Angel Martinez, LF (S)</li><li>Travis Bazzana, 2B (L)</li><li>Patrick Bailey, C (S)</li><li>Brayan Rocchio, SS (S)</li></ol><p>In a sense, the shoe is on the other foot in a sense for this one, as the Guardians will also be using an opener in right-hander Daniel Espino. The White Sox can’t exactly predict what will follow Espino, but are clearly anticipating Cleveland left-hander Foster Griffin in a bulk role.</p><p>As a result, their lineup is a Frankenstein-like mashup of their typical attack versus right-handed starters, followed by a host of their usual weapons for left-handed pitchers. It makes more sense when you see it.</p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-b07bb8e0-c270-11f1-a685-419dc6d789f3" start="1"><li>Sam Antonacci, DH (L)</li><li>Miguel Vargas, 3B (R)</li><li>Munetaka Murakami, 1B (L)</li><li>Kyle Teel, C (L)</li><li>Chase Meidroth, 2B (R)</li><li>Tristan Peters, CF (L)</li><li>Braden Montgomery, RF (S)</li><li>Randal Grichuk, LF (R)</li><li>Colson Montgomery, SS (L)</li></ol><p>Actually, the plan is still a little unclear in looking at it, so perhaps it’s best if Venable explains it.</p><p>“The one thing that we know is that we get Espino up front, so we have the same top four guys,” Venable said. “Second part of our lineup is a little bit of a response to the unknown that's going to follow Espino, and so we have our righties kind of spaced out with a couple lefties in between, and then we'll read and react as the game goes on. We have [Andrew Benintendi] on the bench, [Tommy] Pham, a number of guys -- [Brenton] Doyle that we could pop in different spots.”</p><p>After winning AL Player of the Week in the second-to-last week of the regular season with a barrage that helped keep the Sox in the playoff picture, Miguel Vargas is hitting .154 with no extra-base hits so far this postseason, and Venable acknowledged his All-Star third baseman’s swing was out of sorts in recent days.</p><p>However, Vargas has walked five times in these playoffs and is running a .389 on-base percentage, and seems to be using his plate discipline as a means of getting himself right.</p><p>“At this point it's not about me anymore,” Vargas said. “I try to go out there and help my team the best I can. If it's a walk and get on base for my team, I'm going to do it any time. If it's a stolen bag or driving an RBI, whatever it takes to win a baseball game, I want to be out there and able to do it.”</p>

entries.title: Man charged with 2025 robbery of 82-year-old man in Belmont Cragin
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago man was charged with robbing and battering an 82-year-old man last October in the Belmont Cragin neighborhood. </p><p>Keiber Sandoval Mendoza, 31, faces robbery and aggravated felony charges, Chicago police said. </p><p>On the morning of Oct. 13 last year, Mendoza allegedly approached the man in the 6000 block of West Diversey Avenue and took his property before fleeing, according to police. </p><p>The man suffered a cut to his head and was taken to Advocate Illinois Masonic Medical Center where his condition had stabilized, police said. </p><p>Mendoza was scheduled to appear in court Wednesday. </p>

entries.title: Amazon adquiere almacén vacío en vecindario de West Town para entregas el mismo día
entries.summary: <p>Amazon compró la semana pasada el primer edificio logístico vertical de Chicago para usarlo como centro de entregas el mismo día.</p><p>El gigante del comercio electrónico con sede en Seattle compró el edificio de dos pisos en el 1237 W. Division St. por $195 millones, informó primero Crain’s Chicago Business.</p><p>“Hacer esto nos permite, efectivamente, entregar en cuestión de un par de horas en vez de un par de días y realmente corta esa distancia que cualquier vehículo —ya sea un camión, una van o un carro— necesita recorrer para llegar a los clientes”, dijo Kyle DeGiulio, gerente principal de política de desarrollo económico para el Medio Oeste de Amazon. “Estamos muy emocionados de ampliar nuestra presencia en Chicago”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ad0000" name="module-ad0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Amazon planea comenzar operaciones a finales de 2027 o principios de 2028. La propiedad en West Town, cerca de Goose Island, será un “sub-centro de cumplimiento para entregas el mismo día”, dijo DeGiulio, combinando funciones de almacenamiento y reparto.</p><p>En lugar de usar vehículos de la flota, como las vanes eléctricas de Amazon, las entregas las harán conductores de Amazon Flex —trabajadores que usan sus propios vehículos, al estilo de los conductores de DoorDash o Uber.</p><p>Según DeGiulio, la instalación creará 200 empleos, desde funciones de cumplimiento hasta puestos gerenciales, con un sueldo por hora promedio de cerca de $24. A los empleados de Amazon en Chicago se les ofrecerá la oportunidad de transferirse al sitio de Division Street.</p><p>El almacén será el segundo centro de entregas el mismo día de Amazon en Chicago. La empresa ya tiene un centro similar en Humboldt Park, abierto en 2023, a pesar de la <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2024/11/27/amazon-overcomes-critics-west-humboldt-park-fulfillment-center-community-roots" target="_blank" >ira de los vecinos</a>.</p><p>DeGiulio dijo que la nueva ubicación responderá al creciente apetito de los clientes por entregas el mismo día, especialmente de comestibles y productos farmacéuticos, que la empresa está viendo en Chicago y en todos sus mercados.</p><p>“Hay muchas cosas que la gente quiere de Amazon muy, muy rápido y que están en edificios más lejanos y toman un poco de tiempo”, dijo. “Ahora, al entender un poco el comportamiento del cliente y los tipos de artículos que la gente quiere con rapidez, un sitio como este nos da una mejor oportunidad de atenderlos y además opera en un área donde sentimos que la infraestructura circundante apoya esa operación, en lugar de tratar de poner esto en algún lugar donde no necesariamente encaja”.</p><p>DeGiulio dijo que Amazon llevaba tiempo poniendo los ojos en el área de Goose Island, pero esperaba la oportunidad adecuada. El sitio en Division Street es “muy visible” y resulta atractivo por su rápido acceso a las autopistas. También está cerca de vías como Elston Avenue, lo que permite a los conductores cruzar la ciudad más rápido.</p><p>Reconoció la congestión vehicular de la zona, pero dijo que las inversiones de la Ciudad en infraestructura —como el reemplazo de los dos puentes de Division Street— hicieron que la empresa se inclinara por esa ubicación.</p><p>Logistics Property Co. comenzó la construcción del almacén, de aproximadamente <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/10/24/23415668/west-town-multistory-warehouse-logistics-property" target="_blank" >590,000 pies cuadrados</a>, en 2022. En ese momento, la propiedad era el primer almacén de varios niveles en Chicago, con muelles para camiones en ambos pisos y más de 1,000 espacios de estacionamiento.</p><p>Pero el edificio ha permanecido vacío desde que se terminó en 2024. Logistics Property contrató a la firma inmobiliaria JLL para ayudar a comercializar la propiedad. Logistics Property se negó a comentar.</p><p>Un folleto de mercadeo de JLL y del desarrollador Logistics Property señaló que el edificio está a cinco minutos del Loop y a 15 minutos del Aeropuerto O’Hare. También destacaba una venta estimada de $2,000 millones en comercio electrónico dentro de un radio de 5 millas.</p><p>Amazon posee almacenes de varios niveles en Estados Unidos y en otros países, dijo DeGiulio. Pero esta propiedad es única por su exterior, con murales y una rampa de estacionamiento colorida visible desde la Autopista Kennedy.</p><p>“Es casi como si este edificio hubiera sido construido para que nosotros lo usáramos”, dijo.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: McDonald's sued over AI tool that recommends prices to U.S. franchisees
entries.summary: <p>McDonald’s is facing a federal lawsuit that alleges its AI-enhanced pricing tool violates antitrust laws because it shares nonpublic data with franchisees who might be competing in the same market.</p><p>The lawsuit, which was filed Friday in Illinois, said McDonald’s pricing tool uses artificial intelligence to collect data that competing franchises wouldn’t normally share, like store-level sales. The Chicago-based burger giant has said it makes the tool available to U.S. franchisees to help them set prices at their individual restaurants.</p><p>The lawsuit also blames the pricing system for raising McDonald’s U.S. prices.</p><p>“McDonald’s has built and for years deployed its own information-sharing pricing platform, which draws on data from its millions of daily transactions to set menu prices across thousands of U.S. restaurants,” the lawsuit states. “The result is algorithmic price-fixing aimed at customers who are already stretched thin.”</p><p>McDonald’s said Tuesday that the lawsuit is “filled with inaccuracies” and it would vigorously defend itself.</p><p>“AI does not set menu prices at McDonald’s restaurants — McDonald’s franchisees do,” the company said in a statement. “Optional tools are available to franchisees to help them make the best decisions for their businesses and customers, but these tools do not automate, coordinate or fix pricing in any way.”</p><p>The lawsuit was filed on behalf of DeKalb resident Michael Thomas. According to the lawsuit, Thomas frequently visits McDonald’s and orders a Quarter Pounder with cheese, french fries and a Coke, and he noticed price differences between McDonald’s stores near his home.</p><p>McDonald's said it has used an AI-enhanced pricing tool for more than a decade. The program determines the optimal price for menu items based on a store’s sales, location and other factors, including competitors’ prices.</p><p>McDonald's said that long before adopting the AI-enhanced tool, it collected data and recommended prices to its franchisees, who own and operate 95% of McDonald’s 14,000 U.S. stores.</p><p>“All we do is provide the context of what’s going on,” a McDonald’s spokesperson said. “We don’t have any way to affect the menu pricing in a restaurant.”</p><p>But the lawsuit said McDonald's has “significant leverage over its franchisees” and can pressure them to follow its pricing recommendations.</p><p>The Associated Press left a message Tuesday with the National Owners Association, which represents McDonald’s franchisees.</p><p>McDonald’s has been experimenting with various value strategies in the U.S. and other markets for several years as it tries to win back lower-income consumers, whose visits to fast-food chains have dropped.</p><p>But franchisees don’t always follow its guidance. During a conference call with investors in August, McDonald’s Chairman and CEO Chris Kempczinski said only 60% of its U.S. restaurants were offering McDonald’s proposed menu of 10 items for under $3.</p><p>“As you know, in our system, that’s not something that we just flip the switch on,” Kempczinski said. “It requires conversations with franchisees.”</p><p>The lawsuit asks the judge to certify the case as a class action and to require McDonald's to pay damages to the class. It also seeks to prevent McDonald's from enforcing agreements that restrict competition.</p>

entries.title: Un policía de Chicago fuera de servicio disparó 2 armas al mismo tiempo que dejó heridos en La Villita
entries.summary: <p>Un agente de la Policía de Chicago que estaba fuera de servicio le disparó a una persona mientras disparaba dos armas al mismo tiempo durante una discusión este fin de semana en La Villita, anunció el martes la Oficina Civil de Responsabilidad Policial (COPA).</p><p>Según declaraciones de COPA y del Departamento de Policía de Chicago (CPD), el agente conducía en la cuadra 2600 al oeste de 24th Street y se encontró con un grupo de personas alrededor de las 12:45 a.m. el domingo.</p><p>El agente intercambió palabras con un hombre del grupo y luego disparó un arma “varias veces”, dijeron las autoridades.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-470000" name="module-470000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Después, el agente condujo hacia la cuadra 2300 al sur de Rockwell Street, se bajó de su vehículo y “disparó tiros adicionales desde dos armas de fuego simultáneamente” hacia el área donde había ocurrido la confrontación inicial, dijo COPA. Un hombre recibió dos disparos y fue trasladado al Hospital Mount Sinai en condición estable, informó la policía.</p><p>Inicialmente, la policía describió al hombre como un “agresor” y dijo que había golpeado al policía en la cara durante la discusión. COPA no reportó posteriormente ese detalle.</p><p>El hombre herido fue detenido después del tiroteo, pero más tarde fue liberado sin cargos, dijo la policía. Voceros de la policía no han proporcionado su edad y no pudieron decir de inmediato si seguía hospitalizado.</p><p>Un segundo hombre sufrió una lesión en un brazo y llegó por su cuenta al Hospital Mount Sinai en condición estable, dijo la policía, sin señalar cómo resultó herido.</p><p>El agente fue atendido por lesiones menores y dado de alta del hospital, dijo COPA. Fue puesto en funciones administrativas mientras continúa la investigación de COPA.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

artist Peace Prophet, 70, has created acclaimed works that sell in galleries and art fairs nationwide. Some collectors own hundreds of her paintings. Despite the renown, she remains unhoused — a downtown fixture who paints streetside.</p><p><b>Who is she?</b>: Born Janice Carol Rivers in 1955, Peace Prophet is a longtime painter and mother of four who has struggled with mental illness, according to her family, who say they've tried to give her a better life. Center — Chinatown's polychromatic bonanza of Chinese Eclectic architecture — has received a $750,000 grant to help restore the 98-year-old landmark. The center, 2216 S. Wentworth Ave., is among 24 sites awarded grants through the Save America's Treasures program administered by the National Park Service.</p><p><b>The goal</b>: Pui Tak Center Executive Director David Wu said the award, along with the matching funds the group must raise, will be used to cover big-ticket items such as restoring the center's ornate windows of decorative iron and leaded glass, and repairing the building’s deteriorating roof.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Built in 1928 as the On Leong Merchants Association headquarters and once dubbed Chinatown's "City Hall," the three-story, 36,000-square-foot building was designed by Christian Michaelsen and Sigurd Rognstad, two Norwegian architects who had never been to China. "That period was still under the Chinese Exclusion Act," said historian Anita Luk. "That means during that period, there were not a lot of Chinese architects [in the U.S.] — or maybe none."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydtjltdl-l-p/" The marathon is one of the most renowned in the world, in part because of the city's flat landscape — ideal for record-breaking times.</p><p><b>Start times</b>: Wheelchair and handcycle races are first, beginning at 7:20 a.m. Then some of the world's best runners kick off at 7:30 a.m. and finish in little over 2 hours. Additional waves of runners will start through 8:35 a.m. The average time for a non-elite runner is about 4 hours and 20 minutes. The course closes at 4 p.m.</p><p><b>The route</b>: This year's route differs slightly from last year's, thanks to construction at State and Lake. The 26.2-mile course takes runners through 29 neighborhoods. watched Bob Odenkirk transform from an Emmy-winning comedy writer ("Saturday Night Live") into a drama TV star ("Better Call Saul") and then a silver screen action hero ("Normal").</p><p>Now, the Naperville native is bringing that range to theater – mastering David Mamet's witty banter on the Broadway stage, delivering a powerful rendition of Congressional testimony off-Broadway, and leaning into his silly side in a small production in Champaign this month.</p><p>In an interview with the Sun-Times, Odenkirk, 63, reflected on his 40-year career and his thirst for experimenting and challenging himself.</p><p>"I don’t like living without comedy. ... I loved when that character got to have fun. Those things saved me," Odenkirk said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydtjltdl-l-th/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>How are you coping with soaring gas prices?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). Know what side of the street your loved ones are on. Listen to the crowd; it’s electric!" — <i>Kyle David</i></p><p>"Put your name on your shirt! People will scream your name. That was awesome." — <i>Carol C.</i></p><p>"You'll want to run with the group when the race starts. Don't. Run at your trained/target pace even if it seems like you're dragging. Remain consistent with your plan." — <i>Ryan Jacox</i></p><p>"Leave the headphones at home. Run near the curb and soak in the million people that want to scream support for you for all 26 miles. It's not a race; it's a victory lap for all your hard work. Enjoy!" — <i>Josh Mitzen</i></p><p>"Wear a sweater in the morning that you’re willing to donate. It is cool in the early AM waiting at your coral, the fences will be lined up with the ability to toss your sweater." — <i>Luisa S.</i></p><p>"Avoid the Malört shots." — <i>Jenn M.C.</i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Michael Lansu<br><b>Copy edited by</b>: Satchel Price</p>

entries.title: Bridgeport buzzes with White Sox fans relishing a playoff party 120 years in the making
entries.summary: <p>By the first week of October, the sea of parking lots around Rate Field typically reverts back to asphalt-desert status for its six-month hibernation period.</p><p>That was certainly the case the last four years, with the White Sox piling up 405 losses since their last taste of playoff action in 2021.</p><p>And it’s been that way across the South Side most autumns since President Theodore Roosevelt was in office and the city was still building its way back from the Great Chicago Fire.</p><p>Even in the ten seasons that Sox fans previously got to enjoy fall ball at their home stadium over franchise history, they haven’t experienced the elation of clinching a playoff series at home since Oct. 14, 1906.</p><p>Photos were hard to come by back then, so you can only imagine the scene in the wooden grandstands at long-gone South Side Park near Pershing and Princeton, where Doc White’s complete game sealed a World Series championship over Orval Overall and those pesky Cubs.</p><p>Fast forward 120 years, throw in the grace of a fan in the Vatican, sprinkle in a wand-toting reliever and summon the magic of a gritty young clubhouse — and Sox fans were still buzzing outside the park Wednesday, nearing a South Side party more than a century in the making.</p><p>“We’ve been waiting so long for this,” Nikki Tieman said while tailgating with family and coworkers in Lot C, three hours before first pitch of the Sox’ potential sweep of the Guardians in the American League Division Series.</p><p>“We’re just enjoying it so much because we had a rough couple of years. We were still at the games, and we were still cheering and wearing our gear. But it's just a little sweeter this year,” Tieman said.</p><p>“It’s just a magical year where everything is just magically aligning, so I’m sure the pope is playing some small part.”</p><p>But Tieman’s family has been riding it out with the team since long before Sox fan Rob from Dolton became Pope Leo XIV. The Joliet family had season tickets on the first base line back at old Comiskey Park, well after her uncle Larry Vasquez got his first taste of Sox heartache listening to them on the radio in 1959 when they lost the World Series to the Dodgers.</p><p>“We didn't win, but, you know, I didn't care. I was still rooting,” Vasquez said, sharing an understated, multi-generational angst all too familiar to Sox fans.</p><h3>Following the Sox from afar, in Iraq</h3><p>Tieman’s brother, Miguel Vasquez, was just glad to be able to lock down tickets. He wasn’t able to do that in 2005 while serving in the U.S. Army in Iraq, where the internet left him as frustrated in his quest to buy tickets for his family as it did thousands of Chicago fans this year in the scramble for postseason seats.</p><p>“I tried so hard, but the internet was so bad over there,” Vasquez said, still shaking his head at the failed transaction 21 years after that magical Sox season.</p><p>But his fellow service members knew they couldn’t let a diehard comrade miss out on the magic.</p><p>“I was getting my gear on about to go out, and they stopped, and they're like, ‘Nope. No, you're gonna go watch [World Series-clinching] Game 4,’” Miguel Vazquez said — laughing at the memory of his commanding officer who advised: “You better hope they win because you're not getting another day off.”</p><p>Tailgating regulars John Wisniewski and his father, Rich, were also among the throngs stirring up championship memories in Lot C, hooking a TV up to their pickup to play a recording of that decisive World Series win in Houston.</p><p>“We're trying to get the good vibes from 2005 today,” said the younger Wisniewski, of Algonquin.</p><p>Those vibes were decidedly lacking at their tailgate two years ago for Rich’s birthday during the Sox all-time worst, 121-loss season of 2024. They were the only vehicle in the sprawling lot, while legions of fans lost faith in an organization setting the modern standard for Major League futility.</p><p>“Baseball is home, so for us, it was another day in the park, like, it was great,” John said. “But it was just depressing. And it was just like, we can't wait until we win and can be great again.”</p><p>“I just love to see this,” said Rich, who made a Sox fan out of his son.</p><p>“You don't become a Sox fan. You're born a Sox fan,” John said. “It's your dad, it's your uncle, it's your family — everybody who's a Sox fan, and they bring you here and it just feels like home every time you come.”</p><h3>A crosstown connection</h3><p>Plenty of fans have married into that family, too, like Corey Fennessy, who reluctantly divulges it was a crosstown connection that she made with her husband, Jamie.</p><p>“I obviously married somebody who cared about baseball a lot more than I do,” the former Cubs fan said.</p><p>There’s no doubt about the next generation, either, as the Glen Ellyn couple’s grade school-age son, Mo, declares there’s only one reason for him ever to step foot in Wrigley Field.</p><p>“Only to see the Cubs get smoked,” Mo said, drawing a laugh from his Little League coach dad.</p><p>Being there for Mark Buehrle’s start in Game 2 of the ‘05 Series was great, but Jamie Fennessy has “gotta tell you — this is like the most impactful day.”</p><p>“In 120 years, they haven't done this, and to clinch at home would be what everybody here deserves, because they stuck through thick and thin. It means the world. And, you know, these will be lifelong fans after today,” he said, waving to Mo and his sister, Jane.</p><p>Jamie’s looking forward to an ALCS game with his own dad.</p><p>“We’re just passing it down, doing what's right,” he said. “Baseball kind of brings generations together and it's doing that right now, so it's been awesome.”</p>
entries.author: Mitchell Armentrout

entries.title: Actor, Naperville native Belmont Cameli throws out first pitch at White Sox playoff game
entries.summary: <p>Who would throw out the ceremonial first pitch Wednesday before the Guardians-White Sox playoff game? Inquiring minds wanted to know. The Sox made it sound like a big name would walk out to the Rate Field mound.</p><p>Would it be former President Barack Obama, a noted White Sox fan? Would Pope Leo, the most famous Sox fan in the world, drop in on a pope plane? How about Joakim Noah, who famously asked whether anyone had vacationed in Cleveland? Jim Thome, who starred for both teams? Derrick Rose? Jonathan Toews? </p><p>The answer: none of the above. It was actor Belmont Cameli, a Naperville native.</p><p>All due respect to Cameli and his family, but no one guessed him. </p><p>Cameli, 28, has appeared in the "Saved by the Bell" reboot, the Netflix film "Along for the Ride" and Prime's series "Off Campus," a hockey romance for which he finished shooting the second season this summer.</p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: Mental health system failed woman accused of fatally stabbing 7-year-old girl, lawyer says
entries.summary: <p>A woman accused of fatally stabbing a 7-year-old girl was repeatedly failed by the state’s mental health systems, according to her public defender, who argued this weekend’s tragedy “could have been avoided.”</p><p>Shavon Gayden, 48, was set to appear at an initial court hearing Wednesday, but it was rescheduled for a second time because she remained hospitalized.</p><p>Gayden had a history of committing seemingly random acts of violence — once attacking a CTA bus driver and another time a shelter worker — before she was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/04/vigil-held-for-7-year-old-girl-killed-in-chatham-stabbing" >charged with first-degree murder</a> in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/03/woman-in-custody-after-girl-7-fatally-stabbed-in-chatham" >stabbing death of Eddimar Hernández-Chacón</a> on Saturday.</p><p>Gayden’s attorney, Assistant Public Defender Brett Balmer, told reporters Wednesday that Gayden had repeatedly been hospitalized for psychiatric issues and “never got the help she needed.”</p><p>“Shavon Gayden did not slip through the cracks of a functional system,” Balmer said during a news conference at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse. </p><p>“Shavon Gayden walked right through the open door of a system that does not provide any mental health services [or] sustained treatment for people with psychiatric illness," Balmer added. "This all could have been avoided.”</p><p>Just before noon Saturday, Gayden approached Eddimar and her 17-year-old sister in the 8600 block of South Cottage Grove Avenue and started stabbing the younger girl with a knife, according to police and prosecutors. </p><p>The fatal attack was “unprovoked,” according to an initial police report obtained by the Sun-Times.</p><div class="Enhancement" Hock asked that they wait until Friday to discuss the issue. Balmer also requested access to medical records from up to 10 hospitals where she believes Gayden sought mental health treatment.</p><p>Gayden does not need to be proven “mentally fit” to appear for a detention hearing Friday but will need to be physically present, according to Balmer.</p><p>After court, Balmer repeated an apology Gayden’s mother made to Eddimar’s family, saying she was devastated this happened.</p><p>Gayden’s mother said if her daughter received the help “she tried to get for her, that this wouldn't happen,” according to Balmer. </p><p>“We need to do something in our city because this mental health issue is not going away,” Balmer added. </p><p>Eddimar’s uncle launched a <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/en-memoria-de-eddimar-hernandez-chacon" target="_blank" >GoFundMe</a> campaign which has raised $16,000 as of Wednesday morning. All the money will go towards funeral costs and providing Eddimar a “dignified farewell,” her uncle wrote in Spanish.</p><p>“To our family, Eddimar will always be a very special girl,” he wrote. “Her passing leaves an indescribable void and immense pain for all of us who loved her.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/03/woman-in-custody-after-girl-7-fatally-stabbed-in-chatham" >Woman in custody after girl, 7, fatally stabbed in Chatham</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/04/vigil-held-for-7-year-old-girl-killed-in-chatham-stabbing" >Woman charged in killing of 7-year-old girl has history of jarring attacks</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Bears report: Team practices without 3 O-linemen, 2 RBs
entries.summary: <p>What happened Wednesday at Halas Hall:</p><h3>O-linemen down</h3><p>After playing 89 snaps Sunday, the Bears were bound to find ways to keep their offensive players fresh. Still, it was jarring to see them practice Wednesday without starting guards Joe Thuney and Jonah Jackson and right tackle Darnell Wright. They didn't receive "rest" designations, either — Jackson and Wright have ankle injuries and Thuney has a pectoral muscle injury. All three played every snap against the Jets.</p><p>Quarterback Tyson Bagent said "those guys will hit the field at some point this week."</p><p>The Bears also sat out both running backs Wednesday: Kyle Monangai (thumb/toe) and D'Andre Swift (hip/knee). Coach Ben Johnson said that Monangai's thumb was no concern but his body was sore from the game. </p><p>Defensive tackle Grady Jarrett got a veteran rest day. As expected, quarterback Caleb Williams didn't practice. He has been throwing with teammates, though.</p><p>Johnson said before practice that his staff had a long conversation about how best to practice this week and declared things would be "a little bit different." The Bears were in pads — Johnson considers practicing hard this time of year essential to improvement — though limited some of their offense's work against the scout team Wednesday.</p><h3>Kyler back soon?</h3><p>The Bears have one open spot on their 53-man roster — and it could go to one of three players who are currently on the physically-unable-to-perform list. Chief among them is slot cornerback Kyler Gordon, who returned to practice last week after dealing with a mysterious — and, to his bosses, maddening — calf injury since the spring. Defensive lineman Shemar Turner (knee) and linebacker Noah Sewell (Achilles' tendon) have been practicing even longer. Game 5 is the earliest anyone who starts the season on PUP can play a game.</p><p>"Let’s utilize the time that we have and we’re given, and we’ll make a decision at the end of the week if one of those three are ready to go," Johnson said. </p>

entries.title: City Council grills Amtrak over proposed Bridgeport rail yard
entries.summary: <p>Chicago City Council took up the fight of Bridgeport residents angry about Amtrak's plan to relocate its South Loop rail yard near their homes and replace it with a White Sox stadium.</p><p>Members of the city's Transportation Committee on Wednesday grilled representatives for Amtrak and Sox minority owner Justin Ishbia. The group then passed a resolution opposing Amtrak's plan, and called on the rail company to return at a later date for another hearing.</p><p>No date has been set.</p><p>During the four hour meeting, committee members pressed Amtrak to release an already completed environmental study. Some also shamed the company for closing the deal announced in August out of public view.</p><p>The whole process was begun by Ald. Nicole Lee, whose 11th Ward covers the proposed new Amtrak maintenance site.</p><p>Lee has been leading a coalition of residents who have loudly opposed Amtrak's plans since the rail company <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/08/14/justin-ishbia-white-sox-stadium-amtrak-federal-funding-railyard" target="_blank" >announced them</a> in August. Early last month, Ishbia's company <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" target="_blank" >said it planned</a> a new Sox stadium at the South Loop rail yard site.</p><p>The coalition says it is concerned with the noise and health effects from a 24/7 train facility next door to thousands of people's home. Members say the rail yard should stay on 14th Street, where only a few dozen people live nearby. The coalition wants Amtrak to release its own environmental review. The federal government exempted Amtrak from doing a full environmental study to fast track construction.</p><p>Amtrak says it needs a new rail facility in Chicago, its national hub, to keep its trains up to date and minimize delays. </p><p>Most people attending the meeting thought differently.</p><p>City Council's gallery was nearly filled with opponents of Amtrak's plan. They booed the few public speakers, including representatives for labor unions, who say they approve of Amtrak's plan, which could <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/17/chinatown-and-bridgeport-residents-press-amtrak-leaders-to-pump-the-breaks-on-rail-yard-plan" target="_blank" >bring 3,000 construction jobs</a> and 400 more jobs if the facility opens.</p><p>Amtrak considered rebuilding its outdated maintenance facility at 14th Street, but decided on Canal Street in Bridgeport in 2023, Amtrak representative Steven Segerlin told the committee. He said Amtrak chose the Canal Street site because it was historically a rail yard, close to Union Station, similar in size to the existing yard, and was available for purchase. Keeping the yard at 14th Street would disrupt train service and cost more, he said. Segerlin said this information was shared at <a class="Link" href="https://mwmaintenancefacility.com/viewer.html?d=august-meeting&y=1732" target="_blank" >two previous community meetings</a> in August and September.</p><p>The rail company also plans to relocate the yard's "car wash" for trains, as well as its train storage and train shed. Construction would include updating aging viaducts under the rail yard. Work could begin next year.</p><p>In the meeting, Lee pressed Amtrak to release its own environmental review included in the original grant application. Segerlin said any release would require approval from the U.S. Department of Transportation, which owns Amtrak.</p><p>Ald. Bill Conway (34th) said he looks forward to discussing that further after Amtrak releases the environmental study.</p><p>Ald. Scott Waguespack (32nd) called out Ishbia for not showing up himself.</p><p>In response, Eric Lynn, a representative for Canal Edge, the company behind buying Amtrak's current yard, said he was there to represent Ishbia.</p><p>Ald. Jeylu Gutierrez (14th) said she was disappointed the public learned about this deal after it was completed. </p><p>"Decisions were made behind closed doors without community input," she said.</p>
entries.author: David Struett

entries.title: Mayor Johnson doubles down on his tax-the-rich mantra as budget deadline nears
entries.summary: <p>Two weeks before unveiling what could be his final city budget, Mayor Brandon Johnson is determined to go down fighting by taxing corporations he claims are “making a killing” — and doubling down on his technology taxes.</p><p>The 29-member City Council coalition that rejected Johnson’s corporate head tax has already<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/28/city-council-opposition-pre-election-budget-battle-mayor-brandon-johnson" > established three boundary lines</a> for the preelection budget debate: no property tax increase, no “head tax or tax on job growth” and no counting on money from Springfield not yet approved.</p><p>On Wednesday, Johnson drew his own line in the sand.</p><p>He said he will use his 2027 budget to level the playing field that has allowed corporations to make “more money ... than they’ve ever made in the history of the world," including the "free labor period of slavery," while working people "are standing in lines for food."</p><p>"We're losing our democracy. I talk about Justice [Louis] Brandeis [who said], 'You can either have a democracy or wealth in the hands of a concentrated few, but you can't have both,' " Johnson said. </p><p>“What other approach should I take? I can tell you the approach that I’m going to take. I’m gonna take the approach of the interests of working people to my budget. That is it. That is all,” he said.</p><p>The mayor accused his City Council opposition of "coddling individuals that are already being protected by Donald Trump." And he hinted strongly that he would erase the city’s $882.4 million shortfall by raising the same taxes he used last year to start shifting Chicago’s tax structure to match the digital economy.</p><p>Those taxes include the personal property lease transaction tax on cloud computing, data processing and software platforms otherwise known as the “cloud tax”; a higher tax on online sports betting; and a tax on social media companies that is still the subject of a court challenge — with revenues held in escrow.</p><p>All three tech-oriented taxes are doing better than expected.</p><p>“Are City Council members upset with the PPLT? That’s a tax on corporations. Are they upset with the SMART [social media] tax? That’s a tax on corporations. Even the state did that one. The digital ad tax. That’s a tax on corporations. Are they worried that we’re gonna lose jobs because we have a digital ad tax?” Johnson asked, referring to the tax he has long championed that's now working its way through the Illinois General Assembly.</p><p>“How is it that the state of Illinois can institute a digital ad tax, my social media tax, the PPLT tax — and that doesn’t get any sort of coverage of opposition — but a tax on the largest corporations that benefit from the services that we provide are somehow being attacked? You can’t have it both ways.”</p><p>Johnson opened his news conference by acknowledging what he called the “heartbreaking loss” of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/04/vigil-held-for-7-year-old-girl-killed-in-chatham-stabbing" >Eddimar Paola Hernandez</a>, the 7-year-old girl stabbed to death Saturday in Chatham while walking down the street with her older sister.</p><p>Shavon Gayden, a woman with a history of committing random acts of violence, has been charged with first-degree murder in the attack near 86th Street and Cottage Grove.</p><p>After reaching out to Eddimar's family, Johnson vowed to “show up for them publicly by investing in Chatham and neighborhoods across the city that continue to experience intolerable violence.”</p><p>“We will invest not only in the resources that show up after a tragedy. We will invest in the resources that prevent tragedy from happening at all, because resources are what prevent tragedy,” Johnson said. “I don’t fight for mental health clinics to reopen to appease a nonexistent mental health clinic lobby or for youth jobs because there are well-connected teenagers asking me to do so. I fight for those things because responsible investment in people reduces violence."</p><p>Johnson's tax-the-rich argument is not moving Chicago voters, according to a new poll conducted Sept. 20- 24 by One Future Illinois, a public policy advocacy group that led the charge against Johnson's corporate head tax. </p><p>For the fourth straight month, the mayor's favorability is stuck as 31%, while 68% of the 606 likely Chicago voters surveyed by Change Research rate the mayor as unfavorable. </p><p>Asked how the budget shortfall should be eliminated, 54% of those surveyed said: "Collecting more of the money, fines and fees already owed to the city," while 74% wanted the city to "cut spending before raising taxes and fees." </p><p>Business taxes that include cloud computing and a revived head tax were supported by just 29% of those polled. Only 5% supported raising property taxes.</p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: D'Andre Swift's 'egregious' fumble could cost him vs. Packers, but he's still essential to Bears' offense
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> isn’t about to cast running back D’Andre Swift aside, even after two very costly fumbles this season, and he shouldn’t.</p><p>At his best, Swift has the potential to be the most dangerous player in this offense, and the Bears recognized his blend of hardnosed running between the tackles and big-play capability by giving him a hefty contract extension less than a month ago.</p><p>But there could be some short-term consequences.</p><p>Johnson has been supportive of Swift this week, saying that “nothing needs to be said” to a player like that about those mistakes, but far from forcefully confident. He didn’t answer whether his third-quarter fumble against the Jets, which got him benched the rest of the game, would count against him in game planning for the Packers game Sunday.</p><p>Johnson already has shown no aversion to making an example of someone, and that’s easier to do when there’s a strong contingency like Kyle Monangai.</p><p>Monangai is coming off an overwhelming performance against the Jets with 146 yards and two touchdowns on 30 carries, and Johnson might send a message by starting him or leaning more heavily on him than Swift against the Packers.</p><p>Swift has proven over seven seasons he doesn’t have a fumbling problem — just 13 on 1,233 carries, including playoffs, coming into this season — but both fumbles this season were hard to stomach. He got stripped at the goal line by Vikings defensive lineman Jalen Redmond in Week 2, then coughed up the ball without much upper-body contact against the Jets.</p><p>Johnson split them into two categories Wednesday. He credited Redmond for making a heady play and punching the ball perfectly, but called Swift’s fumble against the Jets “egregious” and pointed loose fundamentals.</p><p>“There’s too many times when the ball’s getting away from our body, and he knows that,” Johnson said. “He takes a lot of pride in it, hence why it’s never been an issue over the course of his career. We’ve got to tighten that up, and he’ll be just fine moving forward.”</p><p>The Bears would ideally have Swift and Monangai working non-stop Sunday.</p><p>Not only are they trying to create margin for backup quarterback Tyson Bagent making his second start of the season, but the Packers have one of the NFL’s worst run defenses. They’ve allowed the fifth-most yards rushing at 139.3 per game and have yet to force a fumble, and the Bears go into the game as the No. 1 rushing team.</p>

entries.title: South Chicago Chapel director denies state charges after rotting bodies found at funeral home
entries.summary: <p>The director of the South Deering funeral home where <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" target="_blank" >56 bodies were found rotting</a> in “deplorable conditions” in August has denied allegations brought against her by the state.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation suspended Johanna Morgan’s funeral director and embalmer license Aug. 5, after investigators discovered bodies in various stages of decomposition at South Chicago Chapel, owned by her husband, Clark Morgan, at 2939 E. 95th St.</p><p>The state accused the Evergreen Park couple of incompetent and untrustworthy funeral practices, unprofessional conduct and violating state regulations.</p><p>On Monday, Johanna Morgan denied all of the allegations against her, except for acknowledging that she was the sole funeral director and embalmer at South Chicago Chapel.</p><p>State regulators, attorneys for the state and for Johanna Morgan held settlement negotiations last month to permanently revoke her license over the grisly funeral home discovery. A formal hearing is scheduled for later this fall.</p><p>The allegations involving South Chicago Chapel are not the first disciplinary action the Morgans have faced.</p><p>Last month, a south suburban cremation storefront business called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/09/25/chicago-police-search-glenwood-business-tied-to-owners-of-south-chicago-chapel" target="_blank" >Planet Green Cremations </a>— owned by the Morgans — was searched as part of a “follow-up” investigation by Chicago police.</p><p>Chicago police officers and Area 2 detectives executed a search warrant at the business at 319 E. Glenwood Lansing Road, which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/28/sisters-mothers-cremated-remains-south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home" target="_blank" >contracted cremation services for families. </a></p><p>Chicago police did not say what was found inside the business, but officers were seen carrying out several boxes.</p><p>In June 2025 they faced disturbingly similar allegations to the South Chicago Chapel situation at their now-shuttered crematory in Chicago Heights, where investigators from the Illinois comptroller’s office found 44 bodies piled up, along with hundreds of sets of mishandled cremated remains.</p><p>The Morgans agreed to shut down Heights Crematory but admitted no wrongdoing under their 2025 agreement with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/06/19/chicago-heights-crematory-bodies-death-license-closed" target="_blank" >the comptroller’s office</a>.</p><p>After shutting down the Chicago Heights business, the comptroller’s office said it “urged” the IDFPR to revoke Johanna Morgan’s funeral director’s license. The office also said it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/grave-injustice/2026/09/25/chicago-police-search-glenwood-business-tied-to-owners-of-south-chicago-chapel" target="_blank" >turned its findings</a> over to law enforcement “in hopes of criminal charges being filed against the Morgans.”</p><p>That case prompted state investigators to visit the Morgans’ South Chicago Chapel in October 2025, though at that time, they found “no serious concerns pertaining to the handling or storing of remains,” according to a timeline provided by Gov. JB Pritzker’s office.</p><p>The couple obtained their respective licenses in the late 1990s, and each faced their first license suspension in 2017 for failing to file state income taxes.</p><p>That year, Johanna Morgan was reprimanded and fined $1,500 for transporting “a decedent across state lines for burial prior to obtaining required permits,” records show. She was also fined $5,000 in 2024 for failing to complete and file three death records “in a timely manner” in 2020.</p><p>The state has filed four tax liens against the couple’s south suburban home, where Evergreen Park police found two bodies inside a double-parked minivan during a bizarre encounter in June 2024.</p><p>Clark Morgan told officers he had picked up the remains from a hospice center and stopped to use the bathroom while en route to the couple’s crematory. Cook County prosecutors later advised police that the incident did not violate state law.</p><p>Illinois State Police said they are still conducting a criminal investigation into the Chicago Heights case and assisting Chicago police with the investigation of South Chicago Chapel.</p>

entries.title: Mujer acusada de matar a niña de 7 años tiene antecedentes de ataques violentos
entries.summary: <p>Una mujer con antecedentes de cometer actos de violencia aparentemente al azar ahora está acusada de apuñalar mortalmente a una niña de 7 años en un ataque “sin provocación” en Chatham durante el fin de semana, según la policía y registros judiciales.</p><p>Shavon Gayden, de 48 años, enfrenta un cargo de asesinato en primer grado por la muerte de Eddimar Hernández Chacón el sábado, según muestran los registros.</p><p>Eddimar y su hermana caminaban por la cuadra 8600 al sur de Cottage Grove Avenue poco antes del mediodía cuando Gayden se les acercó y empezó a apuñalar a Eddimar con un cuchillo, según un reporte de policía inicial obtenido por el Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>El ataque mortal fue “sin provocación”, señala el informe.</p><p>Momentos antes, Gayden había estado dentro de un negocio en Cottage Grove amenazando a una vendedora, dijo en la corte el lunes el fiscal auxiliar del estado Mike Pekara.</p><p>Luego salió y se acercó a Eddimar y a su hermana de 17 años mientras caminaban por la calle tomadas de la mano, dijo Pekara.</p><p>Gayden sacó un cuchillo de su bolsa y primero se abalanzó sobre la hermana mayor, quien logró esquivarla, dijo Pekara. Después Gayden agarró a Eddimar, la tiró al suelo y “comenzó a apuñalarla repetidamente”, según Pekara.</p><p>Una multitud grande y enojada se formó alrededor de la niña mientras yacía desangrándose en la acera, según registros policiales y grabaciones de radio de emergencia. Mientras Gayden se alejaba, un grupo corrió tras ella y al menos una persona la golpeó, dijo Pekara.</p><p>Cuando llegó la policía, Gayden estaba inconsciente pero respiraba, según un reporte de policía. Sufrió una lesión en la sien izquierda y tenía sangrado arterial.</p><p>La confusión reinó mientras los oficiales que respondían intentaban pedir una ambulancia para la caótica escena donde estaba la niña herida.</p><p>“¡¿Dónde está la ambulancia?!”, gritó un oficial a un despachador mientras otros intentaban detener la hemorragia de Eddimar levantándole la cabeza.</p><p>La ambulancia duró unos 10 minutos en llegar, y fue escoltada por la policía hasta el Hospital Infantil Comer. Eddimar fue declarada muerta a la 1:01 p.m. el sábado, informaron las autoridades. Pekara dijo que la niña había sido apuñalada cuatro veces en la espalda.</p><p>La policía recuperó más cuchillos en la bolsa de Gayden, dijo Pekara.</p><p>Gayden fue trasladada al Centro Médico de la Universidad de Chicago. Permanecía hospitalizada con una lesión en la cabeza y no asistió a la audiencia judicial del lunes. La audiencia de detención fue pospuesta al miércoles.</p><p>Los registros judiciales muestran que el historial criminal de Gayden incluye otros ataques aparentemente aleatorios.</p><p>En septiembre de 2023, Gayden fue acusada de golpear a una empleada de la CTA y amenazarla con “acuchillarla”, según un reporte de policía. En octubre de 2024, se declaró culpable de esos cargos y recibió libertad condicional por dos años.</p><p>Fue arrestada de nuevo por atacar a una trabajadora de un albergue aproximadamente un mes después de su acuerdo de culpabilidad, según los registros judiciales.</p><p>Luego Gayden dejó de presentarse a las audiencias en el caso de la CTA y en febrero de 2025 se emitió una orden de arresto en su contra, según los registros judiciales. La orden seguía activa cuando fue arrestada el sábado.</p><p>Gayden continuó asistiendo a audiencias en el caso posterior y finalmente se declaró culpable de agredir a la trabajadora del albergue, según los registros judiciales. Recibió seis meses de supervisión judicial, que completó en enero.</p><p>La familia de Eddimar se reunió el domingo en el lugar del ataque para recordar a la niña.</p><p>Una <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/en-memoria-de-eddimar-hernandez-chacon" target="_blank" >campaña de GoFundMe lanzada por su tío</a> había recaudado unos $16,500 hasta la tarde del miércoles. Todos los fondos se destinarán a los gastos funerarios y a darle a Eddimar una “despedida digna”, escribió su tío.</p><p>“Para nuestra familia, Eddimar siempre será una niña muy especial”, escribió. “Su partida deja un vacío imposible de explicar y un dolor muy grande en todos los que la amamos”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Nic Claxton injury isn't great for Bulls as start of season is in doubt
entries.summary: <p>A hamstring tweak that won’t offer up any clarity until just before the start of the regular season isn’t ideal for Nic Claxton, but it is the hand that’s been dealt for the center.</p><p>Whether he can answer the bell for the opener in Toronto in two weeks or not, however, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> coach Tiago Splitter sees a key piece to the rebuild in the 27-year-old.</p><p>“I think he’s a great fit,” Splitter said on Wednesday. “I think he can run the court, I think he can protect the rim. His production wasn’t as good as maybe two, three years ago last year. We believe there is a reason behind it, and we just want to have the best Nic we can have.”</p><p>Claxton explained that “reason” early on in camp, admitting that back issues derailed his 2024-25 season, but the Nets commitment to tanking last year was why his minutes were cut into.</p><p>The bad news for the Bulls in the short-term was no Claxton and no Zach Collins (quad) for the preseason opener. Collins could be back very soon, but Claxton is an unknown.</p><p>“Of course it is not great that he’s injured and that’s something we’ve got to be patient with,” Splitter added. “Let him heal and get in good shape. But the way he plays, the way he puts pressure at the rim, rolls, he can leap over the rim, so I think he’s important for our offense and our defense.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Talk isn’t cheap</b></h3><p></p><p>Communication breakdowns on the defensive end have seemingly been a staple in Bulls basketball the previous five seasons, and that’s why Norman Powell is so adamant about putting an end to that and starting new habits.</p><p>A reminder of just why the veteran guard was signed in the summer.</p><p>“Drills are great but as soon as that live play happens you kind of lose that sense and you start to try and anticipate,” Powell said of making sure to stay talking as a team. “Just being on them each and every day that we have to talk, we have to communicate where building winning habits happen. Making sure we’re not having two guys go to one player in different rotations, so just staying on them and reinforcing those winning habits on both ends of the ball.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Remember me?</b></h3><h3></h3><p></p><p>As much as the Bulls try and move off of Patrick Williams, he has 18 million reasons he’s not going anywhere. Then another $18 million next season and an $18 million player option for the year after that.</p><p>So how exactly has he looked in training camp, fighting for a spot at the back end of the rotation?</p><p>“I think it’s hard to evaluate guys from practice,” Splitter said. “We want to see what it looks like when the lights are on and go from there. We know how he plays. I’ve coached against him, so we know where he’s at.</p><p>“He’s doing the right things, doing the things I’ve asked him to do. The role I’m asking him to do he’s getting it done.”</p><p></p><h3><b>King for a day</b></h3><h3></h3><p></p><p>The Bulls honored former broadcaster and three-time NBA champion Stacey King with a moment of silence before Wednesday’s game with the Suns and will do so again in the regular-season home opener. They will also wear a patch starting in the regular season to remember King.</p><p>He <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls/2026/06/07/bulls-announce-former-broadcaster-player-stacey-king-died" >died on June 7 </a>at the age of 59.</p>

entries.title: White Sox pitchers issue 10 walks, hitters strike out 19 times in ALDS Game 3 loss to Guardians
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> manager Will Venable’s ballclub proved him right on Wednesday in Game 3 of the American League Division Series, albeit not in a way he’s likely to appreciate.</p><p>He warned before the series that if his team gave away extra bases to a pesky Guardians team that runs the bases well, they would lose. After sharply defying that axiom in the beginning of their Game 2 win in Cleveland, the Sox and 40,590 ardent supporters were dragged back to reality in a 9-3 home loss in Game 3.</p><p>Sox pitching issued 10 walks to just six strikeouts, including three free passes in a disastrous four-run third that turned a roaring sellout crowd into a very large collection of people in black clothing making anxious noises.</p><p>The owner of a 6.15 ERA after the All-Star break, Bryan Hudson retired just one of the four hitters he faced, with the lone out coming via a Patrick Bailey lineout. Entering after Steven Kwan had already erased an early 1-0 Sox lead with an RBI single, Hagen Smith was rolled out to stop the bleeding four days after getting eight outs to start Game 1.</p><p>Instead, the Sox got a version of Smith akin to the guy who walked the bases loaded at the end of that outing. He walked Jose Ramirez to load the bases before getting Chase DeLauter to bounce into a forceout at home. After threatening the Sox lead with an RBI triple late in Game 2, Jo Adell put the Guardians up for good by bouncing a 1-2 fastball down the right field line for a bases-clearing three-bagger on Wednesday.</p><p>Cleveland would insurance runs in the fifth, eighth and ninth, all enabled by free bases. Ramirez led off the fifth inning with a double off Noah Schultz before stealing third, and racing home on a DeLauter bouncer to second before a drawn-in Chase Meidroth could get the ball home. He victimized the Sox once more in the eighth, kickstarted by a leadoff walk from David Sandlin before a soft single from Bailey put a second runner on. With his team an out away from coming up empty, Ramirez dropped a bloop two-run triple just beyond the grasp of a diving Randal Grichuk, extinguishing most notions of a Sox comeback.</p><p>Davis Martin made his postseason debut in the ninth inning of a game that already had slipped away, issuing a pair of walks that both came around to score, as the Sox defense floundered and allowed a Brayan Rocchio pop to land in short left to plate a run. That effort had a way of emptying out the crowd.</p><p>In an afternoon defined by factors the Sox defied in the first two games rearing their heads, the Guardians pitching staff had the fourth-highest strikeout rate in MLB this year, while Sox hitters had the third-highest. Those forces combined to mute the home team's offensive efforts.</p><p>An early opportunity to break the game open in the first when three of the first four Sox hitters reached, the last of which being a Kyle Teel RBI double, was held at one run by strikeouts. Foster Griffin’s inning-ending strikeout of Tristan Peters was the first of a Guardians postseason franchise record seven punchouts in a relief appearance. The Sox struck out 19 times in all, including both Colson and Braden Montgomery when the Sox were held to a single run after Meidroth and Peters led off the fourth with doubles.</p><p>And then there was just rotten luck. Teel ripped a 100 mph liner to right with two runners on and one out in the fifth, only for Guardians second baseman Travis Bazzana to make a leaping catch on his liner and double off Miguel Vargas at second to end the threat.</p><p>Vargas had a chance at redemption with two outs and the bases loaded in the sixth, after Antonacci had just forced a run home by taking a slider off his foot. The Sox All-Star third baseman rallied from down 0-2 before rifling a full-count Hunter Gaddis heater toward the six-hole, but Ramirez knocked it down. Even without catching it cleanly, the Guardians venerable third baseman scrambled to his feet and uncorked a clean throw to first in time to stave off disaster.</p><p>Somewhere in that moment, was a metaphor for this ALDS as it heads to a Game 4 on Thursday.</p>

entries.title: Former Joliet police officer charged over alleged Flock camera misuse
entries.summary: <p>A now former Joliet police officer has been accused of abusing the Flock license plate reader database, according to Illinois State Police.</p><p>Jeremy Harrison, 50, faces a charge of computer tampering and official misconduct in Will County, according to Illinois State Police, which conducted the investigation after accusations were made against Harrison. </p><p>Court documents say the alleged offense occurred July 23, 2025, when Harrison was serving as a lieutenant with the Joliet Police Department.</p><p>Investigators offered no other details on the case. Harrison is due back in court Nov. 17, per court records.</p><p>Harrison makes for at least the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/01/illinois-cities-halt-flock-use-suspend-officers-and-review-policy-amid-alleged-improper-use" target="_blank" ><u>third known case of a law enforcement being accused of misusing the database</u></a> that tracks millions of drivers’ real-time locations in Will County this year.</p><p>Fellow Will County municipality Channahon said it was reviewing its use of Flock cameras after an investigation found that its officers may also made unauthorized searches. The accused officers were placed on leave as an investigation continues.</p><p>Around the same time, a Will County sheriff’s deputy was placed on administrative leave amid allegations he misused the technology, leading southwest suburban Homer Glen to announce it was suspending the use of Flock cameras within its borders “pending final determination of the investigation and review of the Sheriff’s ALPR protocol.”</p><p>It also comes a day after similar charges were leveled against now former Itasca cop Marisa Ciccola and ex-West Chicago officer Gerardo Solis, which prompted West Chicago also to review its use of the technology. Ciccola alone is charged with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/06/former-itasca-west-chicago-police-officers-charged-over-alleged-misuse-of-flock-cameras" target="_blank" ><u>13 felony counts of official misconduct and eight counts of computer tampering</u></a> for allegations she made unauthorized searches multiple times over the span of a year.</p><p>Earlier this year, part-time Prairie Grove officer William Copp, who was also serving as the chief of police for Holiday Hills, was accused of abusing the system to stalk people he knew via <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/20/former-holiday-hills-police-chief-charged-with-making-nearly-300-unauthorized-searches-court-records" target="_blank" ><u>nearly 250 unauthorized searches of their license plate movements</u></a>. Copp also faces multiple felony official misconduct charges.</p><p>Frank McGrath, a former Kenosha County sheriff’s deputy, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/27/flock-license-plate-reader-alpr-chicago-suburb" target="_blank" ><u>charges</u></a> in August after an internal audit revealed he’d used Flock to spy on a co-worker, according to the agency.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/06/former-itasca-west-chicago-police-officers-charged-over-alleged-misuse-of-flock-cameras" >Former Itasca, West Chicago police officers charged with felony misuse of Flock cameras</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/01/illinois-cities-halt-flock-use-suspend-officers-and-review-policy-amid-alleged-improper-use" >Illinois suburbs halt Flock use, suspend officers and review policy amid alleged improper use</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/27/flock-license-plate-reader-alpr-chicago-suburb" >Flock license plate readers turn Chicago suburbs into ground zero for bitter fight over surveillance</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Obama Foundation and Presidential Center workers to unionize: ‘We don't even have a seat at the table’
entries.summary: <p>Nearly four months after the Obama Presidential Center opened, workers are organizing a union, citing "increasing workloads" and benefit rollbacks that have stirred concerns about their future with the organization.</p><p>In a <a class="Link" href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1nSOV8PYbTRxZ2UykW44vxfYmtbNCe8it/view" target="_blank" ><u>letter</u></a> distributed to colleagues on Wednesday morning, the workers allege that foundation leadership has met their concerns with “vague responses.” As a result, the letter states the Obama Foundation and Obama Presidential Center have a “high turnover rate” and workers “continue to leave, taking with them their institutional knowledge and expertise.”</p><p>The union did not have numbers on how many employees have left since the center opened in June, but it represents workers across a wide range of roles, from museum greeters and ticket takers to behind-the-scenes staff who put together exhibits or work in development, communications and marketing.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2e0000" Employees Council 31. Obama Workers United will represent more than 250 workers across the presidential center campus in Chicago, at the Obama Foundation’s offices in Washington, D.C. and remote workers around the U.S.Addressed to colleagues, the letter invites employees to sign their union cards to push for senior leadership to recognize the group’s right to organize “and not waste resources on anti-union messaging, anti-union lawyers, or anti-union meetings.”</p><p>Anders Lindall, director of public affairs for AFSCME Council 31, said that the organizing committee is circulating union cards to co-workers, getting them signed and having conversations to bring as many workers into the union as possible.</p><p>“Generally everybody wants a voice,” Lindall said. “That extends to compensation and conditions in the workplace and more.” He said that workers recently learned they’d get no pay increases this winter while their healthcare costs go up, paid time off was reduced and promotions were suspended.</p><p>Luke Gilday, an Obama Foundation employee and member of the union organizing committee who is based in Washington, D.C., added his signature to the open letter. He said that there is no timeline for securing a union contract with the Obama Foundation, but the focus now is on building momentum.</p><p>Starting at 7 a.m. on Wednesday, workers from the Obama Presidential Center and Obama Foundation stood outside to greet colleagues coming in for their shifts and hand out buttons, stickers and copies of the open letter. Some even posed for selfies with large union signs sporting the logo of their union, Obama Workers United.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> entries.title: Bears QB Tyson Bagent ready for 'one of the greatest rivalries in all of sports'
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Tyson Bagent has seen Lambeau Field from the sideline, but never the spotlight.</p><p>That changes Sunday.</p><p>“To say this is just like any game just wouldn't be true,” he said Wednesday, two days after coach Ben Johnson confirmed he'd start against the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/07/dandre-swifts-egregious-fumble-could-cost-him-vs-packers-but-hes-still-essential-to-bears-offense" target="_blank" >Packers</a>. “This is one of the greatest rivalries in all of sports. It's easy for the fans to get up for, easy for us to get up for. So it will certainly be a different feel out there.”</p><p>The Bears hope Bagent’s efficient performance against the Jets was a prelude to a game that carries extra meaning every year inside Halas Hall. It helps that he's catching the Packers defense at a vulnerable time, too. The Packers give up 139.3 rushing yards per game, the fifth-most in the NFL. Their 26.3 points per game allowed are the 10<sup>th</sup>-most. They have the NFL’s fourth-worst third down percentage and the NFL’s worst red zone percentage. They give up touchdowns 86% of the time their opponent gets to the 20.</p><p>Micah Parsons, who during the offseason targeted Sunday as a potential return date from his torn ACL, has yet to practice with the team. Linebacker Edgerrin Cooper, who was having perhaps the best season of any Packers defender, tore his Achilles’ tendon Sunday.</p><p>Still, Johnson is wary of the Packers’ safeties — and what new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon does with them, typically rotating them from a blanket coverage right before the snap. That will challenge Bagent, who until Sunday had gone three years without a regular-season snap.</p><p>“We've got to very disciplined having our eyes in the right spots …” Johnson said. “Our route runners have got to be in the right spots, as well.”</p><p>The Bears trust Bagent to change plays at the line of scrimmage, based on what he sees from the Packers. They want him to trust his receivers to make plays deeper down the field. Johnson said there were a few plays Sunday in which Bagent threw short when a deeper option was open. The one that Bagent said “really sticks out egregiously” — a deep crossing route he should have thrown to Luther Burden in the third quarter.</p><p>“It would be encouraging from the coaching staff to him, 'You get the green light, man,'” Johnson said. “We have a lot of confidence in how our pass catchers are playing right now. I thought they did a nice job going up for the ball when given an opportunity last week. And so we're going to need more of that this week.”</p><p>Despite the fact he eclipsed Johnson’s stated goal of a 70% completion percentage, Bagent’s play against the Jets was far from perfect. He went 25-for-34 for 268 yards but threw the Jets their first interception in 21 games. He threw three more interceptions that came back because of penalty — though one was a shot play after the Jets jumped offside that he would not have tried otherwise.</p><p>The Bears have long believed that Bagent could start elsewhere. Their rivals agree.</p><p>“I see a really good quarterback,” coach Matt LaFleur told Packers reporters. “He throws with anticipation. He gets the ball out of his hands. He goes to the right spots. I know he’s their backup, but he could start for many teams in the league.”</p><p>Sunday might be Bagent’s last chance to state that case. Quarterback Caleb Williams still isn’t practicing but has been throwing with teammates on the side as he works his way back from a hamstring injury.</p><p>He’ll face an environment unlike any he’s seen before. His games at Div. II Shepherd University were played in front of maybe 5,000 fans, even when they lined up to the rival Shippensburg Red Raiders. The Superdome is the loudest venue he’s played in as a pro — as a rookie in 2023, he threw three interceptions and fumbled the ball in the fourth quarter of a 24-17 loss to the Saints. The only other NFL road game he’s started came against the Chargers — and SoFi Stadium might have had just as many Bears fans.</p><p>“He's just got to figure out what he did well [and] keep doing that, and then the things that we need to improve on, we'll improve on,” Johnson said. “It doesn't matter home or away or who we're playing — that's really the name of the game."</p><p>Bagent is a different quarterback than he was as a rookie. Johnson made that clear when he gave him a two-year, $10 million contract extension a year ago.</p><p>“He carries himself extremely well.— his preparation is elite,” receiver Rome Odunze said. “He carries that confidence with him through the building, through the meeting rooms, through practice. I’ve seen that for three years. It’s nothing new to me.”</p><p>The stakes, though, are.</p><p>“I've always treated each game the same — life-or-death, hair-on-fire, just trying to execute to the best of my ability,” Bagent said. “Hopefully, everybody else feels the same."</p>
